knowledge_statements.title: Expression Trees
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rooted-tree representation of a scalar factorable expression, with no sharing of repeated subexpressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). An expression tree for \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is a finite rooted directed tree whose leaves are variables or constants, whose internal nodes are labeled by admissible operations, and whose edges point from operands to their consuming operation. Each node represents the value obtained recursively from its children, and the root represents \(f\). Distinct occurrences of the same syntactic subexpression occupy distinct nodes; hence the representation does not encode shared intermediate values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expression tree recursively represents a factorable function, duplicating every repeated occurrence of a subexpression rather than sharing its intermediate value.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
Every operation is defined on the values supplied by its children.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The recursively evaluated root value equals \(f(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: Scalar function represented at the root

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Represents factorable functions by operator trees and flattens their internal nodes into bounded auxiliary defining equations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: If \(f\) and all \(g_j\) are factorable over a finite operator set \(\mathcal O\), they can be represented by expression trees whose leaves are model variables or constants and whose non-leaf nodes are operators. Under a dependency ordering, each \(\vartheta_k\in\mathcal O\) depends only on variables \(x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1}\), and \(x_{n+q}\) is the auxiliary associated with the objective expression.

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Acyclic Expression Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expression-DAG representation in which a single intermediate node may serve multiple consumers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). A directed acyclic expression graph for \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) is a finite directed acyclic graph whose source nodes are variables or constants and whose remaining nodes are labeled by admissible operations applied to their predecessor values. One designated output node represents \(f\). A node may have several outgoing edges, so one computed intermediate value can be used by multiple successor operations; repeated subexpressions may therefore be represented by one shared node.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An expression DAG represents a factorable function while allowing one intermediate computation to feed multiple later operations.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
The graph is finite and acyclic.
Each operation is defined on its predecessor values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Evaluation in any topological order assigns every node uniquely and returns \(f(x)\) at the output node.

notation.meaning: Function represented by the designated output node

knowledge_statements.title: Evaluation Traces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A dependency-respecting sequence of intermediate assignments for one expression graph and one input.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an acyclic expression graph with noninput nodes \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_m\}\), an evaluation trace at \(x\in X\) is a sequence \((v_{i_k},z_{i_k})_{k=1}^m\) such that every predecessor of \(v_{i_k}\) occurs earlier or is an input node, and \(z_{i_k}=\phi_{i_k}((z_j)_{j\in\operatorname{pred}(i_k)})\). The final component associated with the designated output node is the represented function value \(f(x)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An evaluation trace lists intermediate assignments in dependency order and ends with the represented function value.
assumptions_latex: The expression graph is finite and acyclic.
\(x\in X\), and every node operation is defined along the trace.

children.title: Topological Factor Orderings
children.top_down_role: Dependency-respecting arrangements of factor evaluations.

knowledge_statements.title: Topological Factor Orderings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear orderings of factor nodes compatible with every data-dependency edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed acyclic expression graph \(G=(V,E)\), a topological factor ordering is a bijection \(\pi:V\to\{1,\ldots,|V|\}\) satisfying \(\pi(u)<\pi(v)\) whenever \((u,v)\in E\). Equivalently, each noninput factor is placed after all factors that supply its operands. Processing nodes in increasing \(\pi\)-order therefore defines every required predecessor value before the corresponding factor is evaluated.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A topological factor ordering places every factor after all factors on which it directly depends.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite directed acyclic graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A topological ordering \(\pi\) exists and supports dependency-valid node evaluation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically standard and fits Topological Factor Orderings, but no cited section, theorem, definition, or page supports either the graph-theoretic statement or its factorable-programming interpretation.

children.title: Ordering Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Structural consequences of alternative valid evaluation arrangements.

knowledge_statements.title: Ordering Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Distinguishes exact evaluation invariance from order-dependent relaxation propagation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi\) and \(\sigma\) be topological orderings of the same deterministic expression DAG. Exact node evaluation at any common admissible input \(x\) assigns identical values under both orderings. By contrast, a sequential relaxation procedure that updates or eliminates intermediate domains after each processed factor need not be order invariant: if its update operators \(R_i\) do not commute, then \(R_{\pi(m)}\circ\cdots\circ R_{\pi(1)}\) and \(R_{\sigma(m)}\circ\cdots\circ R_{\sigma(1)}\) may produce different relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact DAG evaluation is topological-order invariant, but sequential relaxation can depend on order when factor-update operators do not commute.
assumptions_latex: Both orders are topological orderings of one deterministic expression DAG.
All exact node operations are defined at \(x\).
Relaxation updates may use order-dependent intermediate domains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact outputs coincide, whereas noncommuting sequential relaxation updates may yield distinct final bounds or feasible relaxations.

notation.meaning: Relaxation update associated with factor i

review_flags: Exact evaluation invariance is standard; the intended class of order-sensitive relaxation operators requires a dedicated source.
Formula requires review for the precise sequential-update convention.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let \(\mathcal{A}\) be a declared collection of arithmetic operations, such as affine combination, multiplication, and reciprocal on nonzero arguments. knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An arithmetic factorization expresses a function through finitely many dependency-ordered arithmetic assignments ending at the function value.

Every operation in \(\mathcal{A}\) is defined on its attained operand domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The designated terminal factor satisfies \(z_m=f(x)\) for all \(x\in X\).

knowledge_statements.title: Intrinsic-Function Factorizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite compositions extending arithmetic factors by a declared library of univariate intrinsic functions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal{A}\) be an arithmetic operation library and \(\mathcal{I}\) a declared family of univariate intrinsic functions with specified domains. All attained arguments must lie in their operation domains, and the designated output factor must equal \(f(x)\) on \(X\).

All factor arguments remain in the domains of their operations.

children.title: Extrema Selection Structures

knowledge_statements.title: Extrema Selection Structures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite min/max selection nodes represented through branch values or absolute-value identities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For real-valued factors \(u_1,\ldots,u_k\) on \(X\), an extrema selection node defines \(z=\max_{1\le i\le k}u_i\) or \(z=\min_{1\le i\le k}u_i\). Binary nodes admit the exact representations \(\max\{u,v\}=(u+v+|u-v|)/2\) and \(\min\{u,v\}=(u+v-|u-v|)/2\); finite extrema are obtained recursively. Thus extrema selections can be incorporated as primitive nodes or reduced to arithmetic and absolute-value factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Finite minima and maxima are selection nodes and can be decomposed recursively using exact binary absolute-value identities.
assumptions_latex: \(u_i:X\to\mathbb{R}\) for \(i=1,\ldots,k\)
\(k\ge 2\) is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The selection output equals the stated pointwise minimum or maximum on \(X\).
review_flags: The identities are standard, but no supplied locator directly supports extrema-selection factorization.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits Extrema Selection Structures, and the displayed binary identities are standard and correct. Nevertheless, no cited source or locator supports their use as the stated factorization representation.

children.title: Absolute-Value Factorizations
children.top_down_role: Expression structures containing absolute-value factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Absolute-Value Factorizations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonsmooth factorization using absolute-value nodes and equivalent binary branch selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real-valued factor \(u:X\to\mathbb{R}\), an absolute-value factor introduces \(z=|u|\), equivalently \(z=\max\{u,-u\}\). Conversely, binary extrema satisfy \(\max\{u,v\}=(u+v+|u-v|)/2\) and \(\min\{u,v\}=(u+v-|u-v|)/2\). Consequently, any finite factorization built from arithmetic operations and binary minimum or maximum nodes can be converted exactly into one built from arithmetic operations and absolute-value nodes, and vice versa.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Absolute value and binary minimum or maximum selections are exactly interrepresentable using arithmetic identities.
assumptions_latex: All factors are real valued on \(X\).
The arithmetic operations appearing in the identities are admissible.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The original and transformed factorizations have identical pointwise outputs on \(X\).
review_flags: The algebraic identities are standard, but no supplied locator directly supports the factorization equivalence.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits Absolute-Value Factorizations, and the pointwise identities are correct. The bidirectional claim for arbitrary finite factorizations depends on the admitted arithmetic and selection grammar and therefore requires a source with a specific locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Smooth Selection Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conditions under which a finite selection of smooth branches is piecewise smooth.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), let \(g_1,\ldots,g_k\) be continuously differentiable on an open neighborhood of \(X\), and let \(s:X\to\{1,\ldots,k\}\) be a selection map. The function \(f(x)=g_{s(x)}(x)\) is in a piecewise-smooth selection regime when \(X\) admits finitely many regions \(R_1,\ldots,R_q\) covering \(X\), each with nonempty relative interior, such that \(s\) is constant on every \(\operatorname{ri}(R_r)\) and switching occurs only on region boundaries where competing branch values agree.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite smooth-branch selection is piecewise smooth when the active branch is constant inside finitely many regions and switches only on tie boundaries.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
Each \(g_i\) is continuously differentiable near \(X\).
The regions \(R_r\) form a finite cover of \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On each \(\operatorname{ri}(R_r)\), the function \(f\) coincides with one continuously differentiable branch.

A dedicated nonsmooth-analysis source is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Full Nodewise Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended formulation assigning a variable and defining constraint to every noninput expression node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider an acyclic factorization with inputs \(x\in X\), noninput nodes \(i=1,\ldots,m\), and equations \(z_i=\phi_i((z_j)_{j\in P_i},x)\). Its full nodewise lifting introduces every \(z_i\) as an explicit variable and imposes all node equations, together with the original constraints written using the designated output variables. Projection of this lifted feasible set onto the original \(x\)-space equals the feasible set defined by direct recursive evaluation, provided every node equation is imposed exactly.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Full nodewise lifting introduces every intermediate factor as a variable and enforces every defining node equation.
assumptions_latex: The factorization is finite and acyclic.
Each node operation is single valued on its attained domain.
All node equations are imposed exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection of the lifted feasible set onto \(x\) is the original feasible set.

children.title: Selective Lifting

knowledge_statements.title: Selective Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extended formulation retaining variables only for a chosen subset of intermediate nodes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an acyclic factorization with noninput node set \(V\), choose \(S\subseteq V\). A selective lifting introduces explicit variables \(z_i\) only for \(i\in S\); every maximal subexpression whose internal nodes lie in \(V\setminus S\) is substituted recursively into the equation of its nearest retained descendant or output constraint. If all substitutions are exact and every retained node equation is enforced, projection of the selectively lifted feasible set onto the original variables equals the feasible set of the unlifted factorization.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Selective lifting keeps only chosen intermediate variables and exactly substitutes eliminated subexpressions into retained equations or outputs.

children.title: Shared-Subexpression Lifting
children.top_down_role: Common intermediate variables for repeated nonlinear factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Subexpression Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: DAG lifting in which identical nonlinear subexpressions use one auxiliary variable.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), and let several factorable expressions contain the same subexpression \(h(x)\). Shared-subexpression lifting introduces one variable \(w_h\) and the single defining relation \(w_h=h(x)\); every occurrence of \(h(x)\) is replaced by \(w_h\). More generally, one variable is assigned to each equivalence class of identical nodes in the expression DAG. The exact lifted formulation projects onto the original feasible set because \(w_h\) is uniquely determined by \(x\), while relaxations of the defining relation are imposed only once and shared by all consumers of \(w_h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated identical nonlinear factors are represented by one shared auxiliary variable, preserving exact projection while avoiding duplicate lifted relations.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
Each repeated occurrence denotes the same function on the same domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_h=h(x)\) replaces every occurrence of \(h(x)\), and projection onto \(x\)-space preserves the original formulation.

knowledge_statements.title: Higher-Order Product Grouping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive binary representations of a multilinear product and their representation-dependent relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(m\geq3\), a grouping of the product \(y=\prod_{i=1}^m x_i\) is a rooted binary tree whose leaves are \(x_1,\ldots,x_m\) and whose internal nodes satisfy \(w_v=w_{v_L}w_{v_R}\); the root equals \(y\). Every grouping is an exact extended representation of the same product. If each bilinear equality is replaced by a domain-dependent convex relaxation, however, the projected relaxation may depend on the tree and on the intermediate bounds. Thus algebraically equivalent groupings need not yield identical or mutually dominating relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multilinear product admits many exact binary groupings, but recursive bilinear relaxations can differ because their intermediate variables and bounds differ.
assumptions_latex: \(m\geq3\)
Finite bounds are available for every leaf and generated intermediate variable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y=\prod_{i=1}^m x_i\) exactly, while generally \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(R_{T_1})\neq\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(R_{T_2})\).

knowledge_statements.title: Expanded Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial expressions represented as explicit sums of monomial terms.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(p:\mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}\) be a polynomial. Its expanded form is the coefficient representation \(p(x)=\sum_{\alpha\in A}c_\alpha x^\alpha\), where \(A\subset\mathbb{N}^n\) is finite, \(c_\alpha\neq0\), and \(x^\alpha=\prod_{i=1}^n x_i^{\alpha_i}\), after like monomials have been combined. Products of nonmonomial sums are distributed, so the top-level operations are addition of scalar multiples of monomials. This definition concerns algebraic form, not the choice of subsequent lifting or relaxation.

assumptions_latex: \(p\in\mathbb{R}[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Expressions retaining nontrivial products of lower-complexity factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A factored form of a function \(p\) on \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is an algebraically equivalent expression assembled from products of nonconstant factors without fully distributing those products over sums. The designation concerns the retained expression structure; distinct factorizations of the same polynomial are distinct factorable representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Rationalized Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Quotient representations with explicit denominator domains and removable common factors canceled when appropriate.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:D\to\mathbb{R}\). A rationalized form of \(f\) is an expression \(f(x)=p(x)/q(x)\) on a declared domain \(D\subseteq\{x:q(x)\neq0\}\), obtained by algebraic transformations such as collecting fractional terms, replacing division by an explicit reciprocal, or multiplying numerator and denominator by a common nonzero expression. Algebraic equality is asserted only where every original and transformed denominator is nonzero. Cancellation of a common factor therefore preserves the function on the common domain but does not silently restore points excluded by the original expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rationalized form expresses a function as an explicit quotient and records denominator restrictions so algebraic transformations do not alter its domain.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
All original and transformed denominators are nonzero on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f(x)=p(x)/q(x)\) for every \(x\in D\), with \(q(x)\neq0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The domain-preserving quotient formulation is mathematically sensible and definition is an appropriate content kind, but no citation is supplied. A source is needed to establish that this is the intended meaning of rationalized form in the factorable-representation taxonomy rather than a different rationalization convention.

knowledge_statements.title: Form-Dependent Relaxation Strength
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of projected relaxations generated from algebraically equivalent expression graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) be algebraically equivalent expressions on \(D\), and construct \(R(E_k,D)\) by recursively relaxing each nonlinear node using bounds propagated through that expression graph. Exact equivalence of \(E_1\) and \(E_2\) does not imply equality of their projected relaxations. For minimization, \(E_1\) yields a relaxation at least as strong as \(E_2\) precisely when \(\operatorname{proj}R(E_1,D)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}R(E_2,D)\). Without additional structural or bound assumptions, neither inclusion need hold; strength must be compared on the common original-variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Algebraically equivalent forms can produce different relaxations; strength is determined by inclusion after projection, and neither form universally dominates without extra assumptions.
assumptions_latex: \(E_1(x)=E_2(x)\) for all \(x\in D\)
Both lifted relaxations use valid node-domain bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E_1\succeq E_2\iff\operatorname{proj}R(E_1,D)\subseteq\operatorname{proj}R(E_2,D)\), and equivalence alone implies no inclusion.

children.title: Primitive versus Aggregated Graph Nodes

knowledge_statements.title: Primitive versus Aggregated Graph Nodes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fine-grained elemental DAGs versus single nodes representing recognized multivariate factors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h:D\to\mathbb{R}\) be factorable. A primitive-node representation decomposes \(h\) into a DAG whose internal nodes are elementary unary or binary operations and introduces defining relations for their intermediate values. An aggregated-node representation retains \(w=h(x_S)\) as one multivariate graph relation over the variables \(x_S\) on which \(h\) depends. Both are exact when all defining equalities are enforced. Their relaxations can differ because the primitive construction intersects local node relaxations, whereas the aggregated construction may use a relaxation of the full graph of \(h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factor may be decomposed into elementary graph nodes or retained as one multivariate node; exact forms agree, but available relaxations can differ.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\)
Every primitive operation is defined on its propagated domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,w}G_{\mathrm{prim}}=\operatorname{graph}_D(h)=G_{\mathrm{agg}}\) for exact graphs, but this equality need not persist after relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Natural Interval Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Interval evaluation obtained by replacing each operation in an expression by its interval counterpart.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(e\) be a real factorable expression defining \(f\) on a box \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\). Its natural interval extension \([e](X)\) is obtained by replacing each variable by its component interval, each constant by a degenerate interval, and every arithmetic or elementary operation by a valid interval extension, following the syntax tree of \(e\). If all intermediate operations are defined on their interval arguments, inclusion isotonicity gives \(f(X)=\{f(x):x\in X\}\subseteq[e](X)\). Different expressions for the same function may have different natural interval extensions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Natural interval evaluation follows an expression tree with interval operations, enclosing the true range but potentially changing under algebraically equivalent rewrites.
assumptions_latex: \(X\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is a box
Every interval operation encountered by \(e\) is defined.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{f(x):x\in X\}\subseteq[e](X)\).

children.title: Affine Range Forms

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Range Forms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine-arithmetic enclosures retaining correlations through shared noise symbols.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An affine range form for a scalar quantity is \(\widehat z=z_0+\sum_{i=1}^m z_i\varepsilon_i\), where each \(\varepsilon_i\in[-1,1]\); its interval range is \(z_0+\sum_{i=1}^m z_i[-1,1]\). Input variables are encoded with shared noise symbols, affine operations propagate coefficients exactly, and a nonlinear operation replaces its remainder by one or more additional bounded noise terms. If each nonlinear remainder bound is valid, the resulting form encloses every attainable value. Reusing a noise symbol preserves the represented dependence across multiple occurrences of the same uncertain input.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine range forms propagate linear dependence using shared bounded noise symbols and add new symbols only to enclose nonlinear remainders.
assumptions_latex: \(\varepsilon_i\in[-1,1]\)
Every nonlinear approximation is supplied with a valid remainder bound.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(z\in\{z_0+\sum_{i=1}^m z_i\varepsilon_i:\varepsilon_i\in[-1,1]\}\subseteq z_0+\sum_{i=1}^m z_i[-1,1]\).

children.title: Dependency-Retention Comparison

knowledge_statements.title: Dependency-Retention Comparison
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of dependency information retained by interval, centered, and affine range evaluations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For repeated occurrences of an uncertain variable, natural interval evaluation generally treats the resulting interval operands independently. A centered form retains first-order dependence through the common displacement \(X-c\), while an affine form retains linear dependence through shared noise symbols. Consequently, exact cancellations such as \(x-x=0\) are preserved by a shared affine encoding but natural interval subtraction gives \(X-X\), which is nondegenerate when \(X\) is. This dependency advantage does not establish universal width dominance for nonlinear expressions, because derivative, linearization, and remainder bounds can offset it.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Centered and affine forms retain selected variable dependence that natural intervals lose, although this does not guarantee uniformly narrower nonlinear range bounds.
assumptions_latex: \(X=[\underline x,\overline x]\) with \(\underline x<\overline x\)
Repeated occurrences use one shared affine symbol.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \([x-x]_{\mathrm{aff}}=[0,0]\subsetneq X-X=[\underline x-\overline x,\overline x-\underline x]\).

notation.meaning: Range obtained from a shared affine form

assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is nonempty

source_refs.locator: 1.4 Deterministic Global Optimization: Approaches and Classes of Problems p. 18

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a nonempty feasible set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\), a bounded factor \(h:D\to\mathbb{R}\), and a tolerance \(\epsilon\geq0\). For the minimization problem, compute certified values \(a_\ell\leq\ell^*:=\inf_{x\in D}h(x)\leq b_\ell\) with \(b_\ell-a_\ell\leq\epsilon\). For the maximization problem, compute certified values \(a_u\leq u^*:=\sup_{x\in D}h(x)\leq b_u\) with \(b_u-a_u\leq\epsilon\). Output \(L_h=a_\ell\) and \(U_h=b_u\). Then \(h(D)\subseteq[L_h,U_h]\). If both auxiliary problems are solved exactly, output \([\ell^*,u^*]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Globally minimize and maximize the factor, retain a certified lower bound on its infimum and a certified upper bound on its supremum, and return these as an outer range enclosure.

children.title: Bounded Rectangular Domains
children.top_down_role: The canonical domain regime for recursive factorable relaxation.

assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb{N}\) is finite.
\(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) have finite components and satisfy \(\ell\le u\) componentwise.
Any stated range enclosure \([f^L,f^U]\) is assumed valid and finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(X=[\ell,u]\) is a nonempty compact rectangular domain, and a supplied finite interval \([f^L,f^U]\) is a valid enclosure precisely when \(f^L\le f(x)\le f^U\) for every \(x\in X\).

notation.meaning: valid finite range enclosure of a factor

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-dimensional boxes used to initialize and recursively propagate factor ranges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(n\in\mathbb{N}\), and let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb{R}^n\) have finite components satisfying \(\ell_i\le u_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\). A bounded rectangular domain is the box
\[X=[\ell,u]:=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^n:\ell_i\le x_i\le u_i\text{ for every }i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}\}.\]
The box \(X\) is nonempty and compact. For a factor \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\), a finite interval \([f^L,f^U]\) is a valid range enclosure when \(f^L\le f(x)\le f^U\) for every \(x\in X\). Recursive factorable relaxation rules may use any such supplied enclosure; existence of a finite enclosure requires, in addition, that \(f\) be bounded on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded rectangular domain is a nonempty compact finite-dimensional box. A finite interval is a valid range enclosure for a factor when it bounds every factor value on the box; such an enclosure exists only when the factor is bounded there.
knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Rectangular Domains

children.title: Sign-Stable Domains
children.top_down_role: Domains on which factor signs and reciprocal validity are fixed.

knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Stable Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Fixed-sign range conditions for products and reciprocal primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a factor \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) have a valid interval enclosure \([f^L,f^U]\). Its domain is sign-stable when either \(f^L\ge0\) or \(f^U\le0\); thus the sign of \(f(x)\) cannot change on \(X\), although zero may occur. The reciprocal primitive \(1/f\) is range-valid on the entire domain precisely under the stronger condition \(0\notin[f^L,f^U]\), equivalently \(f^L>0\) or \(f^U<0\). For several factors, sign stability means that this predicate holds separately for every factor whose sign is used by a relaxation rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factor is sign-stable if its range is wholly nonnegative or nonpositive. A reciprocal additionally requires the range to exclude zero strictly.
assumptions_latex: \([f^L,f^U]\) is a valid enclosure of \(f(X)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Sign stability is \(f^L\ge0\) or \(f^U\le0\); reciprocal validity is \(f^L>0\) or \(f^U<0\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The sign-stability condition is standard, but exclusion of zero from a merely valid, potentially non-tight enclosure is sufficient rather than necessary for the actual reciprocal to be well-defined on the domain. The stated equivalence becomes necessary only if the interval is the exact factor range, or if 'validity' is explicitly restricted to certification from that enclosure. No source is supplied to resolve the intended formulation.

children.title: Shape-Regime Geometry

children.title: Monotonicity Regions
children.top_down_role: Domain regions classified by directional behavior of intrinsic factors.

knowledge_statements.title: Monotonicity Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regions on which coordinatewise derivative signs remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f\) be continuously differentiable on an open set containing \(D\). A coordinatewise monotonicity region for \(f\) is a set \(D\) for which, for every coordinate \(i\), one fixed alternative holds throughout \(D\): \(\partial_i f(x)\ge0\) for all \(x\in D\), or \(\partial_i f(x)\le0\) for all \(x\in D\). Under the first alternative \(f\) is nondecreasing in coordinate \(i\) along every axis-parallel segment in \(D\); under the second it is nonincreasing.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A monotonicity region is a convex region where each selected partial derivative has a fixed nonnegative or nonpositive sign.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex.
\(f\) is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Fixed signs of \(\partial_i f\) determine coordinatewise monotonicity on \(D\).

notation.meaning: partial derivative of the factor with respect to coordinate i

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The derivative-sign criterion is mathematically standard, but the cited convexity-preservation section is not an inspectable direct locator for coordinatewise monotonicity. The LaTeX statement quantifies over every coordinate, whereas the plain statement refers to selected coordinates. A direct source is needed before choosing and aligning the intended definition.

children.title: Curvature Regions
children.top_down_role: Domain regions classified by convex or concave shape.

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature Regions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Regions on which a twice differentiable factor has fixed convex or concave curvature.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be convex and let \(f\) be twice continuously differentiable on an open set containing \(D\). A convex curvature region for \(f\) satisfies \(\nabla^2 f(x)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in D\); a concave curvature region satisfies \(\nabla^2 f(x)\preceq0\) for every \(x\in D\). Consequently, the restriction \(f|_D\) is respectively convex or concave. A region on which neither semidefinite condition holds uniformly is not a fixed-curvature region under this definition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A curvature region is a convex region where the Hessian is uniformly positive semidefinite or uniformly negative semidefinite.
assumptions_latex: \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) is convex.
\(f\) is twice continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Uniform Hessian semidefiniteness makes \(f|_D\) convex or concave, respectively.

notation.meaning: Hessian of the factor at x

children.title: Shape-Regime Intersections
children.top_down_role: Subdomains induced by simultaneous shape classifications.

knowledge_statements.title: Shape-Regime Intersections
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common refinement of monotonicity, curvature, and primitive-domain regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(M\) be a monotonicity region of a factor \(f\), let \(C\) be a convex or concave curvature region of \(f\), and let \(B\) be a rectangular factor domain. The associated shape-regime cell is
\[R=B\cap M\cap C.\]
If \(R\ne\varnothing\), every derivative-sign condition valid on \(M\), every Hessian semidefiniteness condition valid on \(C\), and every bound condition valid on \(B\) remains valid on \(R\). A finite family of such intersections forms a common refinement on which one relaxation rule may be selected without mixing incompatible shape assumptions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Intersecting box, monotonicity, and curvature regions creates cells where all inherited range and shape conditions hold simultaneously.
assumptions_latex: \(B,M,C\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) are regions for the same factor \(f\).
The defining conditions of \(B\), \(M\), and \(C\) hold pointwise.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: On every nonempty \(R=B\cap M\cap C\), all three families of conditions hold simultaneously.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The inheritance of pointwise conditions under intersection is correct, and representation is an appropriate content kind. However, the claim that a finite family of such cells supports relaxation-rule selection is a nontrivial methodological statement with no source locator.

children.title: Affine Operations

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-aware propagation of convex underestimators and concave overestimators through affine combinations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose \(f_i^L\le f_i\le f_i^U\) on a convex domain \(X\), where \(f_i^L\) is convex and \(f_i^U\) is concave. For \(h=a_0+\sum_{i=1}^m a_i f_i\), define
\[h^L=a_0+\sum_{a_i\ge0}a_i f_i^L+\sum_{a_i<0}a_i f_i^U,\qquad h^U=a_0+\sum_{a_i\ge0}a_i f_i^U+\sum_{a_i<0}a_i f_i^L.\]
Then \(h^L\) is convex, \(h^U\) is concave, and \(h^L(x)\le h(x)\le h^U(x)\) for every \(x\in X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine combinations propagate relaxations by using lower bounds for positive coefficients and upper bounds for negative coefficients, with the choices reversed above.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex.
For each \(i\), \(f_i^L\le f_i\le f_i^U\) on \(X\), with \(f_i^L\) convex and \(f_i^U\) concave.
\(a_0,a_1,\ldots,a_m\in\mathbb{R}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(h^L\le h\le h^U\) on \(X\), with \(h^L\) convex and \(h^U\) concave.

notation.meaning: convex underestimator and concave overestimator of factor i
propagated relaxations of the affine combination

children.title: Sum Operations
children.top_down_role: Additive aggregation of factor relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Sum Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Additive propagation of convex and concave factor relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f,g:X\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(f^L\le f\le f^U\) and \(g^L\le g\le g^U\) on a convex set \(X\), with lower relaxations convex and upper relaxations concave. For \(h=f+g\), set
\[h^L=f^L+g^L,\qquad h^U=f^U+g^U.\]
Then \(h^L\) is convex, \(h^U\) is concave, and \(h^L(x)\le h(x)\le h^U(x)\) for all \(x\in X\). The same rule extends to any finite sum by termwise addition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The lower relaxation of a sum is the sum of lower relaxations; the upper relaxation is the sum of upper relaxations.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex.
\(f^L,g^L\) are convex underestimators and \(f^U,g^U\) are concave overestimators on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^L+g^L\le f+g\le f^U+g^U\) on \(X\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extraction-grounded finite-dimensional convexification bound for finite Minkowski sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let $S_1,\ldots,S_m\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n$. For every $x\in\operatorname{conv}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m S_i\right)$, there exists $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\}$ with $|I|\leq n$ such that \[x\in\sum_{i\notin I}S_i+\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{conv}(S_i).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For every point in the convex hull of a finite Minkowski sum of subsets of R^n, all but at most n summands can be taken from the original sets; only the exceptional summands need convexification.
assumptions_latex: m\in\mathbb{N}
S_i\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\quad(i=1,\ldots,m)
x\in\operatorname{conv}\left(\sum_{i=1}^m S_i\right)
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,m\},\ |I|\leq n:\quad x\in\sum_{i\notin I}S_i+\sum_{i\in I}\operatorname{conv}(S_i).
knowledge_statements.title: Shapley–Folkman Theorem

directory_assessment.rationale: The Sum Operations node is a legitimate application-specific cross-index for additive relaxation calculus, while the general theorem's primary home remains convex analysis.

children.title: Difference Operations
children.top_down_role: Subtractive aggregation of factor relaxations.

knowledge_statements.title: Difference Operations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sign-aware relaxation propagation for subtraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f,g:X\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfy \(f^L\le f\le f^U\) and \(g^L\le g\le g^U\) on a convex set \(X\), with lower relaxations convex and upper relaxations concave. For \(h=f-g\), define
\[h^L=f^L-g^U,\qquad h^U=f^U-g^L.\]
Then \(h^L\) is convex, \(h^U\) is concave, and \(h^L(x)\le h(x)\le h^U(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). Thus subtraction reverses the lower and upper roles of the subtracted factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a difference, subtract the second factor's upper relaxation below and its lower relaxation above.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex.
\(f^L,g^L\) are convex underestimators and \(f^U,g^U\) are concave overestimators on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f^L-g^U\le f-g\le f^U-g^L\) on \(X\).

children.title: Cancellation-Sensitive Assembly
children.top_down_role: Additive structures whose relaxation behavior is affected by cancellation.

knowledge_statements.title: Cancellation-Sensitive Assembly
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of exact cancellation when identical subexpressions are relaxed independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the same factor \(f:X\to\mathbb{R}\) occur twice in \(h=f-f\), and suppose only the common bounds \(L\le f(x)\le U\) are propagated, with \(L<U\). Treating the two occurrences independently under the difference rule yields
\[L-U\le h(x)\le U-L,\]
although algebraically \(h(x)=0\) for every \(x\in X\). Hence independent recursive assembly fails to preserve cancellation and has relaxation width \(2(U-L)\). Sharing the repeated factor or simplifying the expression before relaxation restores the exact enclosure \([0,0]\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Independent relaxation of f minus itself gives a nonzero-width interval, while shared-expression recognition or algebraic simplification gives the exact value zero.
assumptions_latex: \(L\le f(x)\le U\) for all \(x\in X\).
The two occurrences are propagated independently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Independent assembly gives \([L-U,U-L]\), whereas exact cancellation gives \(h(X)=\{0\}\).

notation.meaning: common lower and upper bounds for the repeated factor

knowledge_statements.title: Bounded Bilinear Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: McCormick convex-hull representation for one bilinear term over a rectangle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\), \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), with finite bounds, and let \(w=xy\). The convex hull of the bilinear graph over this rectangle is described by the bounds together with
\[w\ge \ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y,\qquad w\ge u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y,\]
\[w\le u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y,\qquad w\le \ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y.\]
Thus these four affine inequalities give the exact convexification of \(\{(x,y,w):w=xy\}\) over the bounded rectangle.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Four McCormick inequalities describe the convex hull of a bilinear graph over a bounded rectangle.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x,u_x,\ell_y,u_y\in\mathbb{R}\) are finite.
\(\ell_x\le u_x\) and \(\ell_y\le u_y\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed polyhedron equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y,xy):x\in[\ell_x,u_x],\ y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Sign-Structured Product Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Product range placement under fixed factor-sign patterns.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\) and \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\). The exact product range is
\[[\min S,\max S],\qquad S=\{\ell_x\ell_y,\ell_xu_y,u_x\ell_y,u_xu_y\}.\]
Sign stability identifies the active corners without changing the McCormick graph inequalities. For example, if \(0\le\ell_x\le u_x\) and \(0\le\ell_y\le u_y\), then \(xy\in[\ell_x\ell_y,u_xu_y]\). If \(0\le\ell_x\le u_x\) and \(\ell_y\le u_y\le0\), then \(xy\in[u_x\ell_y,\ell_xu_y]\). The remaining fixed-sign regimes follow by symmetry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact product range comes from four corner products; fixed factor signs determine which corners provide its lower and upper endpoints.
assumptions_latex: \(x\) and \(y\) range independently over finite closed intervals.
The stated simplifications use the indicated fixed-sign bounds.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(xy\in[\min S,\max S]\), with endpoint formulas simplified by the factor-sign regime.

notation.meaning: set of the four rectangular corner products

children.title: Fixed-Factor Product Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Fixed-Factor Product Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact affine reduction when either factor interval has zero width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\), \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), and \(w=xy\). If \(\ell_x=u_x=c\), then the bilinear graph reduces to
\[x=c,\qquad w=cy,\qquad \ell_y\le y\le u_y.\]
Accordingly, the McCormick inequalities collapse to the equality \(w=cy\), so their relaxation is exact. Symmetrically, if \(\ell_y=u_y=d\), the graph is given by \(y=d\) and \(w=dx\). This conclusion holds for constants of any sign, including zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When one product factor is fixed, the bilinear term becomes affine and the McCormick relaxation is exact.
assumptions_latex: The factor bounds are finite.
Either \(\ell_x=u_x=c\) or \(\ell_y=u_y=d\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A fixed factor converts \(w=xy\) into an affine equality, and the product envelope equals the graph.

children.title: Zero-Width Product Domains

knowledge_statements.title: Zero-Width Product Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degeneracy of a bilinear graph when either factor interval has zero width.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\), \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), and \(z=xy\). If \(\ell_x=u_x=c\), then the product graph is \(\{(c,y,cy):y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\}\). If \(\ell_y=u_y=d\), it is \(\{(x,d,dx):x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\}\). In either case, the four McCormick inequalities imply the corresponding affine equality, so the relaxation equals the product graph and has no relaxation gap.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Fixing either factor collapses the bounded bilinear graph to an affine graph, and the McCormick relaxation becomes exact.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell_x\le u_x\) and \(\ell_y\le u_y\).
At least one of \(u_x-\ell_x\) and \(u_y-\ell_y\) equals zero.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(\ell_x=u_x=c\), then \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y,xy):(x,y)\in[c,c]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\}=\{(c,y,cy):y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\}\). If \(\ell_y=u_y=d\), the analogous set is \(\{(x,d,dx):x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\}\).

children.title: Exact Product Envelopes

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Product Envelopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact convex and concave envelopes of a bilinear term over a rectangle.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(f(x,y)=xy\) on \(B=[\ell_x,u_x]\times[\ell_y,u_y]\), the exact envelopes are
\[f^{\mathrm{cv}}(x,y)=\max\{\ell_x y+\ell_y x-\ell_x\ell_y,\;u_x y+u_y x-u_xu_y\},\]
\[f^{\mathrm{cc}}(x,y)=\min\{u_x y+\ell_y x-u_x\ell_y,\;\ell_x y+u_y x-\ell_xu_y\}.\]
Consequently, the convex hull of the graph is described by \(f^{\mathrm{cv}}(x,y)\le z\le f^{\mathrm{cc}}(x,y)\) together with \((x,y)\in B\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The four McCormick planes give the exact convex and concave envelopes, hence the convex hull of a bounded bilinear graph.
assumptions_latex: \(-\infty<\ell_x\le u_x<\infty\).
\(-\infty<\ell_y\le u_y<\infty\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{conv}\{(x,y,xy):(x,y)\in B\}=\{(x,y,z):(x,y)\in B,\ f^{\mathrm{cv}}(x,y)\le z\le f^{\mathrm{cc}}(x,y)\}\).

notation.meaning: Convex and concave envelopes on the rectangle.

knowledge_statements.title: Single-Curvature Intrinsics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact univariate envelopes when curvature has one sign throughout the active interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=[a,b]\) with \(a<b\), and let \(s(x)=((b-x)\phi(a)+(x-a)\phi(b))/(b-a)\) be the endpoint secant. If \(\phi:I\to\mathbb R\) is convex, then \(\phi^{\mathrm{cv}}=\phi\) and \(\phi^{\mathrm{cc}}=s\). If \(\phi\) is concave, then \(\phi^{\mathrm{cv}}=s\) and \(\phi^{\mathrm{cc}}=\phi\). Thus a single-curvature intrinsic has one exact nonlinear envelope and one exact affine envelope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On an interval, a convex or concave intrinsic is one envelope itself; its opposite envelope is the endpoint secant.
assumptions_latex: \(I=[a,b]\) is compact with \(a<b\).
\(\phi\) is finite and either convex or concave throughout \(I\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Convex \(\phi\) gives \((\phi^{\mathrm{cv}},\phi^{\mathrm{cc}})=(\phi,s)\); concave \(\phi\) gives \((\phi^{\mathrm{cv}},\phi^{\mathrm{cc}})=(s,\phi)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Curvature-Changing Intrinsics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact envelope representation for a continuous intrinsic crossing curvature regions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For continuous \(\phi:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\), including functions whose curvature changes on \([a,b]\), its exact envelopes satisfy
\[\phi^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)=\min\{\lambda\phi(u)+(1-\lambda)\phi(v):u,v\in[a,b],\ \lambda\in[0,1],\ \lambda u+(1-\lambda)v=x\},\]
\[\phi^{\mathrm{cc}}(x)=\max\{\lambda\phi(u)+(1-\lambda)\phi(v):u,v\in[a,b],\ \lambda\in[0,1],\ \lambda u+(1-\lambda)v=x\}.\]
The optimizing pair may lie in distinct curvature regions, producing supporting secants across intervening arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact envelopes of a curvature-changing univariate function arise from optimal chords, possibly joining points in different curvature regions.
assumptions_latex: \([a,b]\) is a nonempty compact interval.
\(\phi:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed minimum and maximum equal the convex and concave envelopes of \(\phi\) on \([a,b]\).

notation.meaning: Convex-combination weight locating the chord value at x.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonmonotone Intrinsics
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact interval range accounting for interior turning points of a smooth intrinsic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(\phi:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and differentiable on \((a,b)\), and define \(S=\{a,b\}\cup\{x\in(a,b):\phi'(x)=0\}\). If \(S\) is nonempty and compact, then
\[\min_{x\in[a,b]}\phi(x)=\min_{x\in S}\phi(x),\qquad \max_{x\in[a,b]}\phi(x)=\max_{x\in S}\phi(x).\]
Hence endpoint evaluation alone is generally invalid for a nonmonotone intrinsic; every interior stationary point capable of attaining an extremum must be included in its range relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The exact range of a smooth nonmonotone intrinsic is determined by endpoints and interior stationary points, not endpoints alone.
assumptions_latex: \(\phi\) is continuous on \([a,b]\) and differentiable on \((a,b)\).
The endpoint-and-stationary-point set \(S\) is compact.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\phi([a,b])=[\min_{x\in S}\phi(x),\max_{x\in S}\phi(x)]\).

notation.meaning: Set of interval endpoints and interior stationary points.

knowledge_statements.title: Reciprocal Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact envelopes of the reciprocal on an interval separated from zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=[a,b]\) with either \(0<a<b\) or \(a<b<0\), and let \(r(x)=1/x\). Its endpoint secant is \(s(x)=(a+b-x)/(ab)\). On a positive interval, \(r\) is convex and \((r^{\mathrm{cv}},r^{\mathrm{cc}})=(r,s)\). On a negative interval, \(r\) is concave and \((r^{\mathrm{cv}},r^{\mathrm{cc}})=(s,r)\). These are the exact univariate envelopes on \(I\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Away from zero, reciprocal curvature is fixed: the reciprocal is one exact envelope and its endpoint secant is the other.
assumptions_latex: Either \(0<a\) or \(b<0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Positive \(I\) gives \(r^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)=1/x\) and \(r^{\mathrm{cc}}(x)=s(x)\); negative \(I\) reverses these assignments.

notation.meaning: Affine secant through the reciprocal endpoint values.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factorable relaxation of a bounded quotient using reciprocal and product auxiliaries.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(q=x/y\) with \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\), \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\), and \(0\notin[\ell_y,u_y]\), introduce \(r=1/y\) and \(q=xr\). Bound \(r\) by the ordered endpoint values of \(1/y\); impose the exact reciprocal envelopes for \((y,r)\), then impose the four McCormick inequalities for \((x,r,q)\). Every quotient-graph point satisfies this extended formulation, so its projection is a valid convex relaxation of the fractional factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bounded quotient with denominator separated from zero can be relaxed by composing reciprocal envelopes with a McCormick product relaxation.
assumptions_latex: \(x\in[\ell_x,u_x]\) and \(y\in[\ell_y,u_y]\) have finite bounds.
\(0\notin[\ell_y,u_y]\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The projection of the reciprocal-plus-product extended formulation contains \(\{(x,y,q):q=x/y\}\) over the stated box.

children.title: Singularity-Separated Domains
children.top_down_role: Factor domains partitioned away from denominator singularities.

knowledge_statements.title: Singularity-Separated Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Domain condition ensuring bounded reciprocal and nondegenerate quotient primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A denominator interval \(Y=[\ell_y,u_y]\) is singularity-separated precisely when \(0\notin Y\), equivalently when \(\ell_y>0\) or \(u_y<0\). Then \(\delta=\min_{y\in Y}|y|>0\), the reciprocal is finite on \(Y\), and \[|1/y_1-1/y_2|\le \delta^{-2}|y_1-y_2|\qquad(y_1,y_2\in Y).\] If \(0\in Y\), the reciprocal is undefined at zero and unbounded on \(Y\setminus\{0\}\). Moreover, a quotient graph \(q=x/y\) is unbounded near zero whenever the numerator domain contains a nonzero value; treating such a domain requires excluding the singularity, commonly by subdivision or disjunction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A denominator interval supports bounded reciprocal relaxation exactly when it stays a positive distance from zero; quotient graphs with a possible nonzero numerator are otherwise unbounded near zero.
assumptions_latex: \(Y=[\ell_y,u_y]\) is a nonempty compact interval.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(0\notin Y\iff \delta:=\min_{y\in Y}|y|>0\), which makes \(y\mapsto1/y\) bounded and Lipschitz on \(Y\).

notation.meaning: Distance of the denominator interval from zero.

knowledge_statements.title: Integer-Power Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature and domain regimes for integer powers used as factorable primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(p_n(x)=x^n\) with \(n\in\mathbb Z\), the cases \(n=0\) and \(n=1\) are constant and affine. If \(n\ge2\) is even, \(p_n\) is convex on \(\mathbb R\). If \(n\ge3\) is odd, it is concave on \(( -\infty,0]\) and convex on \([0,\infty)\). If \(n<0\), its domain is \(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\); it is convex on \((0,\infty)\), while on \(( -\infty,0)\) it is convex for even \(n\) and concave for odd \(n\). Thus interval envelopes must respect parity, sign, and whether zero is excluded or crossed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Integer-power curvature depends on exponent parity and interval sign, and negative powers require intervals that exclude zero.
assumptions_latex: \(n\in\mathbb Z\).
The active interval lies within the real domain of \(x^n\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Even positive powers are globally convex; odd positive powers change curvature at zero; negative powers require singularity-separated domains and have parity-dependent curvature on the negative component.

children.title: Real-Power Factors

knowledge_statements.title: Real-Power Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Curvature classification of real powers on the standard positive domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a real exponent \(\alpha\), define \(p_\alpha(x)=x^\alpha\) on \((0,\infty)\). Since \(p_\alpha''(x)=\alpha(\alpha-1)x^{\alpha-2}\), the function is convex when \(\alpha<0\) or \(\alpha>1\), concave when \(0<\alpha<1\), affine when \(\alpha=1\), and constant when \(\alpha=0\). For \(\alpha>0\), the continuous extension \(p_\alpha(0)=0\) is available; for \(\alpha<0\), zero remains a singularity.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On positive arguments, real-power curvature is determined by the sign of α(α−1), while negative exponents are singular at zero.
assumptions_latex: \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\).
\(x>0\), except when the stated continuous extension at zero is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The sign of \(\alpha(\alpha-1)\) gives the complete curvature classification of \(x^\alpha\) on \((0,\infty)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Exponent-Sensitive Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Real-domain rules for power primitives as determined by exponent type and sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). The standard real-valued power \(x^\alpha\) is always defined for \(x>0\). If \(\alpha=n\in\mathbb Z\), its domain is \(\mathbb R\) for \(n\ge0\) and \(\mathbb R\setminus\{0\}\) for \(n<0\). If \(\alpha=p/q\) is nonintegral in lowest terms, negative bases are admitted exactly when \(q\) is odd, and zero is admitted exactly when \(p>0\). For irrational \(\alpha\), the ordinary real domain is positive, with the continuous value zero optionally adjoined when \(\alpha>0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The admissible real domain of a power depends on whether its exponent is integer, rational with odd denominator, irrational, positive, or negative.
assumptions_latex: For rational exponents, \(p/q\) is in lowest terms with \(q>0\).
Powers use their ordinary single-valued real interpretation.

\[s_j^{\mathrm{cv}}(p)\leq s_j(p)\leq s_j^{\mathrm{cc}}(p)\quad\text{for every }p\in P.\]
These component pairs may be used as atomic inner relaxations in any generalized composition rule whose hypotheses they satisfy.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite acyclic expression graph, let \(I\subseteq V\) be its input-node set, and let \(x=(x_v)_{v\in I}\) be the input vector. For every \(v\in V\setminus I\), let \(y_v=\phi_v(y_{\operatorname{pa}(v)})\), and choose a relation \(R_v\) containing the exact graph of \(\phi_v\) over the prescribed argument bounds. With \(y_v=x_v\) for \(v\in I\), define
\[\mathcal R_G=\left\{(x,y):y_v=x_v\ \text{for every }v\in I,\ (y_{\operatorname{pa}(v)},y_v)\in R_v\ \text{for every }v\in V\setminus I\right\}.\]
For any designated output node \(o\in V\), the projection of \(\mathcal R_G\) onto \((x,y_o)\) contains the exact graph of the input-output function represented at \(o\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A nodewise graph relaxation introduces a variable for every expression node, imposes a valid local graph relaxation at each noninput node, and yields an outer approximation after projection to the inputs and designated output.

knowledge_statements.title: Shared-Subexpression Formulations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Directed-acyclic lifted formulation using one auxiliary variable for each repeated subexpression.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose several locations in a factorable model use the same subexpression \(g(x)\). A shared-subexpression formulation represents all occurrences by one node and one auxiliary variable \(y_g\), with one relaxed graph relation for \(y_g=g(x)\); every consumer uses that same \(y_g\). Equivalently, start from a formulation having copies \(y_g^1,\ldots,y_g^r\) and impose
\[y_g^1=y_g^2=\cdots=y_g^r.\]
The shared formulation is the projection of this equality-coupled copied formulation. Omitting those equalities generally produces a weaker outer approximation because distinct consumers may otherwise select incompatible relaxed values of the common expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeated subexpressions share one auxiliary variable, preserving consistency across all consumers and potentially strengthening the relaxation compared with independent copies.
assumptions_latex: All represented occurrences are algebraically the same function \(g\) of the same underlying variables.
The local relation imposed for \(y_g=g(x)\) is a valid outer approximation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: One shared variable is equivalent to equality-coupled copies and is at least as strong as the corresponding uncoupled copied relaxation.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite acyclic expression graph with input-node set \(I\subseteq V\) and designated output-node set \(O\subseteq V\). Choose a set \(S\subseteq V\setminus(I\cup O)\) of intermediate nodes to lift, and introduce an auxiliary variable \(y_v\) for each \(v\in S\cup O\). For every \(v\in S\cup O\), recursively substitute the expressions at predecessors outside \(S\cup I\) to obtain a function \(\psi_v^S\) of the input variables and the retained predecessor variables. Choose a relation \(R_v^S\) containing the exact bounded graph of \(\psi_v^S\), and define
\[\mathcal R_{G,S}=\left\{(x,y):(x,y_{S\cap\operatorname{pred}(v)},y_v)\in R_v^S\ \text{for every }v\in S\cup O\right\},\]
where \(y_{S\cap\operatorname{pred}(v)}\) denotes all retained predecessor values on which \(\psi_v^S\) depends. This is a partial auxiliary-variable model, and its projection onto the input and output variables contains the exact input-output graph represented by \(G\).

knowledge_statements.title: Nonlinear Reduced-Space Estimators
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines recursive McCormick estimators expressed solely in the original variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:

\[

\]
Their final formulas contain only \(x\); intermediate computational-graph quantities are evaluated symbolically rather than retained as optimization variables.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced-space estimators recursively bound a factorable function by convex and concave functions of the original variables, without retaining computational-graph variables.

knowledge_statements.title: Affine Support Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linearizes reduced-space estimators at selected reference points.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(f^{\mathrm{cv}}\) and \(f^{\mathrm{cc}}\) bound \(f\) on a convex set \(X\). For \(\bar x\in X\), choose \(g\in\partial f^{\mathrm{cv}}(\bar x)\) and \(h\in\partial^{+}f^{\mathrm{cc}}(\bar x)\). The affine support functions
\[
\ell_{\bar x}(x)=f^{\mathrm{cv}}(\bar x)+g^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x),\qquad
u_{\bar x}(x)=f^{\mathrm{cc}}(\bar x)+h^{\mathsf T}(x-\bar x)
\]
satisfy \(\ell_{\bar x}(x)\le f(x)\le\nu_{\bar x}(x)\) for every \(x\in X\). Finite maxima of lower supports and finite minima of upper supports remain valid piecewise-affine estimators.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Write a factorable expression as an acyclic graph \(z_i=\phi_i(z_{p(i)})\), with original variables among the initial nodes and output \(z_m=f(x)\). knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-Space Tightness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Orders estimator pairs by pointwise dominance on the original domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For two valid reduced-space estimator pairs \((\ell_1,u_1)\) and \((\ell_2,u_2)\) of \(f\) on \(X\), the first pair is at least as tight as the second when
\[
\ell_1(x)\ge\ell_2(x)\quad\text{and}\quad u_1(x)\le u_2(x)
\qquad(x\in X).
\]
It is strictly tighter when at least one inequality is strict at some point. Equivalently, every pointwise interval \([\ell_1(x),u_1(x)]\) is contained in \([\ell_2(x),u_2(x)]\). If neither pair dominates pointwise, their tightness is incomparable under this order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One reduced-space estimator pair is tighter when it gives no lower underestimator and no higher overestimator at every point.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Factor Recognition Effects
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shows how recognizing algebraic dependence can strengthen a factor relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
On \(X=[0,1]\), consider \(f(x)=x(1-x)\). Treating the two factors only through the bilinear McCormick envelope with \(y=1-x\) yields the valid upper estimator
\[
u_{m bil}(x)=\min\{x,1-x\}.
\]
Recognizing the common variable before relaxation identifies \(f(x)=x-x^2\) as concave, so the exact concave overestimator is \(u_{m rec}(x)=x(1-x)\). Consequently \(u_{m rec}(x)<u_{m bil}(x)\) for every \(x\in(0,1)\). Algebraically equivalent factor recognitions can therefore produce strictly different relaxation strength.

knowledge_statements.title: Supporting-Hyperplane Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Constructs solver-facing affine outer models from factor-relaxation subgradients.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(g:X\to\mathbb{R}\) be convex on a convex set \(X\). For each sampled point \(x^k\in X\) and subgradient \(s^k\in\partial g(x^k)\), the inequality
\[
t\ge g(x^k)+(s^k)^{\mathsf T}(x-x^k)
\]
is valid for the epigraph of \(g\). A finite collection yields the polyhedral outer model \(t\ge\max_k\{g(x^k)+(s^k)^{\mathsf T}(x-x^k)\}\). For a concave function \(q\), supergradients analogously give valid inequalities \(t\le q(x^k)+(r^k)^{\mathsf T}(x-x^k)\) for its hypograph.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Univariate secant outer estimators on a bounded interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R\) be convex, where \(a<b\), and define its secant affine function by \[s_{a,b}(x)=\frac{b-x}{b-a}f(a)+\frac{x-a}{b-a}f(b).\] Then \(f(x)\le s_{a,b}(x)\) for every \(x\in[a,b]\). Consequently, \(y\le s_{a,b}(x)\) is a valid outer relaxation of the hypograph relation \(y\le f(x)\), and, for any valid underestimator \(\ell(x)\le f(x)\), the strip \(\ell(x)\le y\le s_{a,b}(x)\) contains the graph relation \(y=f(x)\). If \(f\) is concave, the secant inequality reverses and the secant is a valid underestimator.

knowledge_statements.title: Piecewise-Linear Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polyhedral outer models assembled from finitely many affine estimators.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a factor relation \(y=f(x)\) on a polytope \(X\subset\mathbb R^n\), let affine functions \(\ell_i\) and \(u_j\) satisfy \(\ell_i(x)\le f(x)\le u_j(x)\) on \(X\). A piecewise-linear outer model is \[R=\{(x,y):x\in X,\ \max_{i\in I}\ell_i(x)\le y\le\min_{j\in J}u_j(x)\}.\] Equivalently, it is described by the finitely many linear inequalities \(y\ge\ell_i(x)\) and \(y\le u_j(x)\). It is valid because the graph of \(f\) over \(X\) is contained in \(R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A piecewise-linear outer model sandwiches a factor graph between finite maxima and minima of valid affine estimators.

knowledge_statements.title: Exact Intrinsic Envelopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex and concave envelopes of a bounded-domain univariate factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D=[a,b]\) and let \(f:D\to\mathbb R\) be bounded. The convex envelope and concave envelope of \(f\) on \(D\) are \[\operatorname{vex}_D f(x)=\sup\{g(x):g\text{ is convex on }D,\ g\le f\},\] \[\operatorname{cav}_D f(x)=\inf\{h(x):h\text{ is concave on }D,\ h\ge f\}.\] They are respectively the pointwise greatest convex underestimator and least concave overestimator. Consequently, \(\operatorname{vex}_D f(x)\le f(x)\le\operatorname{cav}_D f(x)\), and no other convex lower or concave upper estimator dominates them in the appropriate direction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The intrinsic envelopes are the tightest convex underestimator and concave overestimator of a factor on its stated interval.

knowledge_statements.title: Aggregated Multivariate Envelopes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint convexification dominates separate convexification of coupled factor relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be compact and let \(F(x)=(f_1(x),\ldots,f_m(x))\). Define the joint graph \(G=\{(x,F(x)):x\in X\}\) and individual graphs \(G_i=\{(x,y_i):x\in X,\ y_i=f_i(x)\}\). Then \[\operatorname{conv}(G)\subseteq\{(x,y):(x,y_i)\in\operatorname{conv}(G_i)\text{ for every }i\}.\] Therefore an exact aggregated multivariate envelope retains correlations among the factor outputs and is never weaker than intersecting their separate graph convexifications. The inclusion may be strict when the outputs share variables or satisfy additional joint relations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Convexifying coupled outputs jointly is at least as strong as intersecting their separate graph convexifications, and can be strictly stronger.

Introducing \(z=T(y)\) gives the exact lifted equivalence \[y=f(x)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad z=(T\circ f)(x),\quad y=T^{-1}(z).\] If recognized convex, concave, or conic descriptions of these transformed relations yield a valid set \(R_T\) containing every lifted triple, then \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(R_T)\) is a valid relaxation of the original factor graph. It is stronger than an existing relaxation \(R\) precisely when \(\operatorname{proj}_{x,y}(R_T)\subseteq R\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An invertible transformation can expose convex structure; projecting any valid transformed lifted model preserves validity and may strengthen the original relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Relaxation strength depends on the chosen factorization and auxiliary-variable graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let two expression-graph decompositions \(D_1,D_2\) represent the same feasible set \(F\subseteq X\), and let \(R_{D_r}\) be valid lifted relaxations with \(F\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(R_{D_r})\). For minimization of \(c(x)\), define \(L(D_r)=\inf\{c(x):(x,w)\in R_{D_r}\}\). A relaxation-oriented selection rule prefers \(D_1\) to \(D_2\) when \(L(D_1)>L(D_2)\), subject to acceptable formulation cost. If \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R_{D_1})\subseteq\operatorname{proj}_x(R_{D_2})\), then \(L(D_1)\ge L(D_2)\) for every common minimization objective; absent containment, decompositions may be incomparable.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Subexpression Recognition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A shared auxiliary variable preserves equality between repeated occurrences of one factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose two occurrences of the same subexpression \(f(x)\) feed relations \(y_1=F_1(f(x))\) and \(y_2=F_2(f(x))\). A shared formulation introduces one auxiliary variable \(w\) and one valid factor relaxation \((x,w)\in R_f\), then uses that same \(w\) in both downstream relations. A duplicated formulation introduces \(w_1,w_2\) with \((x,w_i)\in R_f\) independently. Every shared lifted point maps to a duplicated point by \(w_1=w_2=w\); hence the projection of the shared relaxation is contained in that of the duplicated relaxation. Equality need not hold because independent relaxed copies may take inconsistent values.

Thus algebraically redundant factor relations can only strengthen, or leave unchanged, the relaxation.

knowledge_statements.title: Adaptive Piecewise Refinement
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Selective partition refinement driven by a computable local relaxation-error indicator.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an initial finite partition \(\mathcal P_0\), valid local relaxations \(R(C)\), a tolerance \(\varepsilon>0\), and indicators \(\eta(C)\geq0\). At iteration \(t\), solve the relaxation formed from \(\{R(C):C\in\mathcal P_t\}\); select an active cell \(C_t\) with \(\eta(C_t)>\varepsilon\), replace it by finitely many children whose union is \(C_t\), recompute their factor ranges and relaxations, and set \(\mathcal P_{t+1}=(\mathcal P_t\setminus\{C_t\})\cup\operatorname{child}(C_t)\). Stop when every active indicator is at most \(\varepsilon\), and output the resulting piecewise relaxation and bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly solve the piecewise relaxation, select a cell with excessive estimated relaxation error, subdivide it, and stop when all active errors meet tolerance.
assumptions_latex: Every child family covers its parent cell.
All local relaxations and range enclosures are valid.
The indicator and cell-selection rule are computable.

children.title: Hybrid Relaxation Systems

children.title: McCormick–Interval Hybrids
children.top_down_role: Recursive convex and concave relaxations supported by validated range enclosures.

knowledge_statements.title: McCormick–Interval Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive convex–concave relaxations coupled to validated interval enclosures at every expression node.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each node \(v\) of a factorable expression, associate an interval \(W_v=[\underline w_v,\overline w_v]\) and functions \(w_v^{\mathrm{cv}},w_v^{\mathrm{cc}}\). Leaves use their exact values and ranges. At an internal node \(w_v=\phi_v(w_{p_1},\ldots,w_{p_r})\), first compute a validated interval extension \(W_v\) from the parent enclosures, then apply a valid McCormick composition rule on \(W_{p_1},\ldots,W_{p_r}\). The resulting hybrid satisfies \[w_v^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\leq w_v(x)\leq w_v^{\mathrm{cc}}(x),\qquad w_v(x)\in W_v\] for every feasible \(x\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each expression node carries both a validated interval and McCormick convex and concave bounds; interval information supplies the domains required by recursive composition.
assumptions_latex: Every interval extension encloses the corresponding primitive image.
Every primitive McCormick rule is valid on the supplied parent intervals.
The expression graph is finite and acyclic.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_v^{\mathrm{cv}}\leq w_v\leq w_v^{\mathrm{cc}}\) and \(w_v\in W_v\) at every node.

notation.meaning: Validated interval enclosure at node v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation fits the McCormick–Interval Hybrids container and introduces the required node ranges and estimators, but the recursive hybrid formalism and its validity conditions have no cited source.

children.title: McCormick–Affine Hybrids
children.top_down_role: Recursive relaxations augmented by affine dependency information.

knowledge_statements.title: McCormick–Affine Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive McCormick relaxations augmented by affine forms that retain first-order dependency information.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Represent every intermediate factor by an affine enclosure \(A_v(\xi)=a_{v0}+a_v^{\mathsf T}\xi+[-r_v,r_v]\), where \(\xi\in[-1,1]^q\), together with McCormick bounds \(w_v^{\mathrm{cv}}\) and \(w_v^{\mathrm{cc}}\). Primitive operations propagate both representations: affine arithmetic supplies a dependency-aware enclosure \(W_v\supseteq A_v([-1,1]^q)\), while a valid McCormick rule uses these enclosures and parent relaxations. Intersecting the resulting node relaxation with the inequalities implied by \(A_v\) is valid and cannot enlarge it. Consequently, every feasible factor value remains between the propagated convex underestimator and concave overestimator.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Affine forms track shared dependency symbols while McCormick rules propagate convex and concave bounds; intersecting both valid representations can tighten the recursive relaxation.
assumptions_latex: Affine propagation encloses every attainable factor value.
Primitive McCormick rules are valid on the affine-derived ranges.
All shared noise symbols retain consistent meanings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_v^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\leq w_v(x)\leq w_v^{\mathrm{cc}}(x)\) for every feasible \(x\).

notation.meaning: Vector of shared affine noise symbols

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A representation is appropriate, but no source is supplied for this affine–McCormick hybrid. A source is also needed to establish how the shared noise symbols are consistently linked to original variables and how affine-form constraints are incorporated into the lifted relaxation.

children.title: McCormick–Taylor Models
children.top_down_role: Higher-order local models combined with recursive convex and concave relaxation.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.locator: Higher-order convergent relaxations of factorable functions

knowledge_statements.title: McCormick–Taylor Models
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-order Taylor enclosures whose polynomial and remainder parts receive recursive convex–concave bounds.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: On a box \(X\) about \(x_0\), let a factor admit a validated Taylor model \(w(x)=P_p(x-x_0)+r(x)\) with \(r(x)\in R=[\underline r,\overline r]\). If \(P_p^{\mathrm{cv}}\) is a convex underestimator of \(P_p\) on \(X\) and \(P_p^{\mathrm{cc}}\) is a concave overestimator, then \[w^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)=P_p^{\mathrm{cv}}(x-x_0)+\underline r,\qquad w^{\mathrm{cc}}(x)=P_p^{\mathrm{cc}}(x-x_0)+\overline r\] are valid McCormick bounds. Recursive Taylor-model arithmetic may be used provided every truncation remainder is outwardly enclosed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bound a factor by a finite Taylor polynomial plus a validated remainder interval, then combine polynomial relaxations with the remainder endpoints.
assumptions_latex: \(w(x)-P_p(x-x_0)\in R\) for every \(x\in X\).
The polynomial underestimator and overestimator are valid on \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\leq w(x)\leq w^{\mathrm{cc}}(x)\) for all \(x\in X\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The Taylor-model representation and remainder-endpoint bounds are plausible and locally consistent, but the specialized McCormick–Taylor construction is unsupported by any citation.

children.title: McCormick–Spectral Hybrids
children.top_down_role: Recursive relaxations combined with curvature-based underestimators.

knowledge_statements.title: McCormick–Spectral Hybrids
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive bounds strengthened by Hessian-eigenvalue information on smooth factor subexpressions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(g\in C^2(X)\) on the box \(X=[\ell,u]\), and choose \(\alpha_i\geq0\) such that \(\nabla^2g(x)+2\operatorname{Diag}(\alpha)\succeq0\) for every \(x\in X\). Then \[g^{\mathrm{sp}}(x)=g(x)-\sum_i\alpha_i(\ell_i-x_i)(x_i-u_i)\] is convex on \(X\) and satisfies \(g^{\mathrm{sp}}(x)\leq g(x)\). Therefore the pointwise maximum of \(g^{\mathrm{sp}}\) and any McCormick convex underestimator is another valid convex underestimator. An analogous concave overestimator follows by applying the construction to \(-g\) and negating.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Curvature bounds produce a convex spectral underestimator; taking its maximum with a McCormick underestimator preserves validity and can strengthen the bound.
assumptions_latex: \(g\) is twice continuously differentiable on the box \(X\).
The chosen diagonal shift makes the adjusted Hessian positive semidefinite throughout \(X\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\max\{g^{\mathrm{sp}},g^{\mathrm{cv}}\}\leq g\) on \(X\).

children.title: Range-Enclosure Validity
