knowledge_statements.title: Range-Enclosure Validity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inductive validity of intermediate ranges in a finite factor-expression graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let a finite acyclic expression graph have leaves ranging in prescribed sets \(W_i\). In a topological ordering, suppose every internal node \(v\) computes \(w_v=\phi_v(w_{p_1},\ldots,w_{p_r})\), and its propagated enclosure satisfies \[\phi_v(W_{p_1},\ldots,W_{p_r})\subseteq W_v.\] Then, for every feasible leaf assignment and every node \(v\), the exact recursively evaluated value satisfies \(w_v\in W_v\). The conclusion remains valid after intersecting \(W_v\) with any additional enclosure independently known to contain every attainable value of \(w_v\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If every primitive range operation encloses the image of its parent ranges, all recursively propagated intermediate ranges contain their exact factor values.
assumptions_latex: The expression graph is finite and acyclic.
Leaf ranges contain all feasible leaf values.
Every primitive range extension encloses its image on the parent ranges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_v\in W_v\) for every node \(v\) and every feasible leaf assignment.

notation.meaning: Propagated range enclosure at node v

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem correctly states recursive range-enclosure inheritance on a finite acyclic graph, but no source or explicit standard-field rationale is provided for this nontrivial candidate claim.

children.title: Convex–Concave Validity
children.top_down_role: Validity of recursively propagated underestimators and overestimators.

knowledge_statements.title: Convex–Concave Validity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Inductive inheritance of convex underestimators and concave overestimators through recursive factor composition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be convex and let a finite acyclic factor graph define node functions \(w_v:X\to\mathbb R\). At each leaf, suppose \(w_v^{\mathrm{cv}}=w_v^{\mathrm{cc}}=w_v\). At every internal node, suppose the selected primitive composition rule maps valid parent relaxations and valid parent ranges to a convex function \(w_v^{\mathrm{cv}}\) and a concave function \(w_v^{\mathrm{cc}}\) satisfying the pointwise primitive bounds. Then, at every node, \[w_v^{\mathrm{cv}}(x)\leq w_v(x)\leq w_v^{\mathrm{cc}}(x)\qquad\text{for all }x\in X.\] In particular, the root pair is a valid convex–concave relaxation of the complete expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid primitive composition rules preserve convex underestimation and concave overestimation throughout a finite acyclic factor graph.
assumptions_latex: \(X\) is convex and the factor graph is finite and acyclic.
Leaf relaxations are exact.
Each primitive rule is valid on the propagated parent ranges.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(w_v^{\mathrm{cv}}\leq w_v\leq w_v^{\mathrm{cc}}\) on \(X\) for every node \(v\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem fits the validity-inheritance container and is internally coherent, but the cited section on convex and concave functions does not specifically locate the recursive McCormick composition result. A source with a theorem or section on recursive relaxation propagation is required.

children.title: Factorability Closure
children.top_down_role: Closure of supported expression classes under recursive construction.

knowledge_statements.title: Factorability Closure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Closure of the supported expression class under finite recursive application of admissible primitives.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal F_0\) contain constants and coordinate projections on a domain \(X\), and let \(\Phi\) be a collection of admissible finite-arity primitives. Define recursively \[\mathcal F_{k+1}=\mathcal F_k\cup\{\phi(f_1,\ldots,f_r):\phi\in\Phi,\ f_i\in\mathcal F_k,\ \text{and the composition is defined on }X\}.\] The factorable class \(\mathcal F=\bigcup_{k\geq0}\mathcal F_k\) contains every finite expression tree built from \(\mathcal F_0\) and \(\Phi\), and it is closed under every defined primitive composition. If relaxation rules exist for all primitives, every member of \(\mathcal F\) admits a finite recursive relaxation graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Constants and variables, closed under finitely many supported primitive compositions, form the factorable expression class; primitive relaxation rules then cover every such expression.
assumptions_latex: Every primitive in \(\Phi\) has finite arity.
Only compositions defined throughout the relevant domain are admitted.
A relaxation rule is available for each primitive when the final assertion is used.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_i\in\mathcal F\) and \(\phi\in\Phi\) imply \(\phi(f_1,\ldots,f_r)\in\mathcal F\) whenever defined.

notation.meaning: Expressions of recursive depth at most k

children.title: Partition Monotonicity
children.top_down_role: Ordering of relaxations across nested partition elements.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition Monotonicity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nested domain cells yield nested relaxations when every relaxation rule is restriction-monotone.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(Y\subseteq X\) be nested domain cells and let \(R(D)\) denote a lifted factorable relaxation constructed on a cell \(D\). Assume every propagated range and every primitive relaxation is restriction-monotone, so restricting from \(X\) to \(Y\) cannot enlarge the corresponding lifted set. Then \[R(Y)\subseteq R(X)\cap\{(x,w):x\in Y\}.\] Consequently, if a partition \(\mathcal P'\) refines \(\mathcal P\), the union of child relaxations is contained in the union of their parent relaxations. For minimization, the relaxation lower bound is therefore nondecreasing under refinement.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When range propagation and primitive relaxations respect domain restriction, every child-cell relaxation lies inside its parent relaxation, so minimization bounds cannot decrease upon refinement.
assumptions_latex: Every child cell is contained in its parent.
Range propagation and primitive relaxation rules are restriction-monotone.
The same lifted representation is used before and after refinement.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R_{\mathcal P'}\subseteq R_{\mathcal P}\) and \(L(\mathcal P')\geq L(\mathcal P)\) for minimization.

notation.meaning: Lifted relaxation constructed on cell D

children.title: Degenerate Perfection
children.top_down_role: Exactness on collapsed parameter domains.

assumptions_latex: \(B=\prod_{i=1}^n[\ell_i,u_i]\subset\mathbb R^n\) is a nonempty box.
\(f:B\to\mathbb R\), and \(f_B^{\mathrm L},f_B^{\mathrm U}:B\to\mathbb R\) satisfy \(f_B^{\mathrm L}\le f\le f_B^{\mathrm U}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(f_{\{\bar x\}}^{\mathrm L}(\bar x)=f(\bar x)=f_{\{\bar x\}}^{\mathrm U}(\bar x)\).

notation.meaning: Lower and upper recursive estimators on a box
Collapsed box consisting of one point

review_flags: Exact recursive-relaxation convention requires a factorable-programming source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pointwise exactness when every variable interval collapses to a singleton.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A recursively constructed relaxation is degenerately perfect if, for every \(\bar x\in B\), evaluating the same relaxation rules on the singleton domain \(\{\bar x\}\) yields
\[
f_{\{\bar x\}}^{\mathrm L}(\bar x)=f(\bar x)=f_{\{\bar x\}}^{\mathrm U}(\bar x).
\]
Thus all relaxation width caused solely by domain uncertainty vanishes on a collapsed box.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factorable relaxation is degenerately perfect when its lower and upper estimators both equal the original function on every singleton box.
knowledge_statements.title: Degenerate Perfection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The property fits the Degenerate Perfection container and is internally well formed, but no citation supports the claimed convention for recursively constructed factorable relaxations. The listed inventory does not specifically address singleton-domain exactness.

children.title: Partition Convergence
children.top_down_role: Convergence of relaxations along shrinking partition elements.

assumptions_latex: \(B_k\subset\mathbb R^n\) are boxes with \(x^\ast\in B_k\) and \(\operatorname{diam}(B_k)\to0\).
\(f_{B_k}^{\mathrm L}\le f\le f_{B_k}^{\mathrm U}\) on \(B_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sup_{x\in B_k}(f(x)-f_{B_k}^{\mathrm L}(x))\to0\) and \(\sup_{x\in B_k}(f_{B_k}^{\mathrm U}(x)-f(x))\to0\).

notation.meaning: Nested or otherwise shrinking partition elements
Lower and upper estimators on the current element

review_flags: The stated uniform estimator version needs a factorable-relaxation source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform convergence of lower and upper estimators on shrinking partition elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The relaxation is partition convergent at \(x^\ast\) if every sequence of partition boxes \(B_k\ni x^\ast\) with \(\operatorname{diam}(B_k)\to0\) satisfies
\[
\sup_{x\in B_k}\bigl(f(x)-f_{B_k}^{\mathrm L}(x)\bigr)\to0,
\qquad
\sup_{x\in B_k}\bigl(f_{B_k}^{\mathrm U}(x)-f(x)\bigr)\to0.
\]
Equivalently, the maximum two-sided estimator error vanishes along every such shrinking sequence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Partition convergence means that both estimator errors vanish uniformly on every sequence of partition boxes shrinking to a point.
knowledge_statements.title: Partition Convergence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement matches the partition-convergence role and clearly specifies uniform two-sided estimator error. A source specifically establishing or defining this factorable-relaxation notion is required; the general partition-method inventory is not attached and does not visibly support this exact formulation.

children.title: Envelope Exactness Regimes
children.top_down_role: Settings in which recursive constructions attain exact or stronger convexifications.

children.title: Primitive-Envelope Exactness
children.top_down_role: Exact convexification at individual supported graph nodes.

assumptions_latex: \(D\subset\mathbb R^m\) is compact and convex, and \(\phi:D\to\mathbb R\) is continuous.
The primitive node is represented by an auxiliary variable \(z\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R_\phi=\operatorname{conv}(G_\phi)\).

notation.meaning: Graph of the primitive operation over its node domain
Convex relaxation installed at the primitive node

review_flags: Supported primitive classes and closure conventions require a dedicated source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact graph convexification for one primitive operation on its current domain.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A primitive relaxation is envelope exact on \(D\) precisely when its lifted feasible set equals the closed convex hull of the primitive graph:
\[
\mathcal R_\phi=\operatorname{conv}\bigl\{(y,z)\in D\times\mathbb R:z=\phi(y)\bigr\}.
\]
For a scalar output, this is equivalent to imposing \(\operatorname{vex}_D\phi(y)\le z\le\operatorname{cav}_D\phi(y)\), where the two bounds are the convex and concave envelopes on \(D\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A primitive relaxation is exact when its lifted set is the convex hull of that primitive's graph over the current domain.
knowledge_statements.title: Primitive-Envelope Exactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The condition is appropriate for Primitive-Envelope Exactness, and compactness plus continuity make the graph-hull formulation coherent. No cited source supports the graph-hull and convex/concave-envelope equivalence or identifies the supported primitive-relaxation convention.

children.title: Composition Exactness
children.top_down_role: Composition regimes preserving envelope strength.

assumptions_latex: \(g:X\to I\subset\mathbb R\) and \(h:I\to\mathbb R\), with \(X\) compact and convex.
\(g\) is affine on \(X\), and \(I=g(X)\).
The lifted relaxation of \(h\) on \(I\) is its exact graph convex hull.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R_{h\circ g}=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,z):x\in X,\ z=h(g(x))\}\).

notation.meaning: Inner affine mapping and outer primitive
Exact image of the inner mapping
Projection of the lifted recursive relaxation

review_flags: This sufficient exactness regime needs confirmation from an envelope-composition source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A sufficient scalar-composition regime using an affine inner map and its exact image.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the scalar composition \(f=h\circ g\), suppose \(g\) is affine and the intermediate domain is exactly \(I=g(X)\). If the lifted constraint \((y,z)\in\operatorname{conv}\{(t,h(t)):t\in I\}\) is used together with \(y=g(x)\), then projection onto \((x,z)\) is exact:
\[
\mathcal R_{h\circ g}=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,z)\in X\times\mathbb R:z=h(g(x))\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact outer convexification remains exact after an affine inner map when the outer envelope uses the inner map's exact image.
knowledge_statements.title: Composition Exactness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed exactness is false for a general affine, noninjective inner map on an arbitrary compact convex set. Convexifying the outer graph over g(X) can admit decompositions of g(x) that cannot be lifted to a convex decomposition having barycenter x. Exactness needs stronger hypotheses, such as an appropriate injective affine equivalence or a fiber/decomposition lifting property; the theorem must not be weakened merely to pass review.

children.title: Recursive versus Joint Convexification
children.top_down_role: Gap between sequential primitive relaxation and aggregated-factor convexification.

assumptions_latex: \(f\) is represented by a directed acyclic graph of primitive equalities over a compact domain \(X\).
Each primitive equality is replaced by a convex graph relaxation on a valid intermediate domain.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{joint}}\subseteq\mathcal R_{\mathrm{rec}}\), with strict inclusion possible.

notation.meaning: Projection of the intersection of primitive graph relaxations
Closed convex hull of the complete input-output graph

review_flags: Strict-gap examples and precise lifted-space hypotheses require a factorable-convexification source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison after projecting both formulations to the original input-output space.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{joint}}=\operatorname{conv}\{(x,z)\in X\times\mathbb R:z=f(x)\}
\]
and let \(\mathcal R_{\mathrm{rec}}\) be the projected relaxation obtained by convexifying primitive graph constraints separately. Validity of every primitive relaxation implies
\[
\mathcal R_{\mathrm{joint}}\subseteq\mathcal R_{\mathrm{rec}}.
\]
The inclusion can be strict because separate convexification need not preserve dependencies shared across intermediate variables; equality requires an additional composition-exactness property.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint graph convexification is at least as strong as projected recursive convexification; lost dependencies can make the containment strict.
knowledge_statements.title: Recursive versus Joint Convexification

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The containment has the correct direction when every primitive relaxation is valid and both sets are projected to the same input-output space, and the property fits the container. A factorable-convexification source is still required for the formal projected formulation and the assertion that strict inclusion can occur.

children.title: Pointwise Convergence Orders
children.top_down_role: Local convergence of estimators on shrinking domains.

assumptions_latex: \(B_k\ni x^\ast\) are boxes with \(\delta_k=\operatorname{diam}(B_k)\to0\).
\(f_{B_k}^{\mathrm L}\le f\le f_{B_k}^{\mathrm U}\) on \(B_k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_k=O(\delta_k^p)\).
review_flags: Terminology and error normalization need alignment with a relaxation-order source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniform pointwise estimator error measured against box diameter.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Define
\[
e_k=\sup_{x\in B_k}\max\bigl\{f(x)-f_{B_k}^{\mathrm L}(x),\ f_{B_k}^{\mathrm U}(x)-f(x)\bigr\}.
\]
The estimators have pointwise convergence order at least \(p>0\) along \((B_k)\) if there exist \(C<\infty\) and \(k_0\) such that
\[
e_k\le C\delta_k^p\qquad\text{for every }k\ge k_0.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Pointwise order p means the worst lower-or-upper estimator error on each shrinking box is bounded by a constant times its diameter to p.
knowledge_statements.title: Pointwise Convergence Orders

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: This is a coherent definition of a uniform estimator-error order and fits the local convergence-order container. No authoritative source is cited for calling this the pointwise convergence order or for the chosen boxwise supremum normalization.

children.title: Hausdorff Convergence Orders
children.top_down_role: Setwise convergence of relaxed graphs.

assumptions_latex: \(G_k\) and \(R_k\) are nonempty compact subsets of a common Euclidean space.
\(\delta_k=\operatorname{diam}(B_k)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(d_H(R_k,G_k)=O(\delta_k^p)\).

notation.meaning: Exact graph restricted to the current box
Relaxed graph over the current box
Hausdorff distance in a fixed norm

review_flags: The graph-space scaling convention needs alignment with a relaxation-order source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Setwise graph error in a fixed ambient norm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The relaxed graphs have Hausdorff convergence order at least \(p>0\) along \((B_k)\) if constants \(C<\infty\) and \(k_0\) exist such that
\[
d_H(R_k,G_k)\le C\delta_k^p\qquad\text{for every }k\ge k_0,
\]
where
\[
d_H(A,C)=\max\left\{\sup_{a\in A}\inf_{c\in C}\|a-c\|,\ \sup_{c\in C}\inf_{a\in A}\|c-a\|\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Hausdorff order p means the relaxed graph approaches the exact graph set at rate proportional to the box diameter raised to p.
knowledge_statements.title: Hausdorff Convergence Orders

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is mathematically coherent for nonempty compact graph sets in a fixed ambient norm and fits the Hausdorff-order container. It lacks a source establishing this convention for factorable relaxed graphs and its scaling by input-box diameter.

children.title: Arithmetic Rate Inheritance
children.top_down_role: Convergence-order propagation through addition and multiplication.

assumptions_latex: \(u\) and \(v\) are uniformly bounded on all sufficiently small boxes \(B_k\).
Their valid lower and upper estimators have errors \(O(\delta_k^p)\) and \(O(\delta_k^q)\).
Sum and product estimators use standard interval-consistent arithmetic rules.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_{u\pm v,k}=O(\delta_k^{\min\{p,q\}})\) and \(e_{uv,k}=O(\delta_k^{\min\{p,q\}})\).

notation.meaning: Estimator error for an expression w
Orders of the two operand estimators

review_flags: Exact arithmetic relaxation formulas and sharpness conditions require a dedicated source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rate propagation for bounded scalar operands under standard recursive arithmetic relaxations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
If \(e_{u,k}=O(\delta_k^p)\) and \(e_{v,k}=O(\delta_k^q)\), then addition and subtraction propagate the slower operand rate:
\[
e_{u\pm v,k}=O\bigl(\delta_k^{\min\{p,q\}}\bigr).
\]
If \(u\), \(v\), and their enclosures are uniformly bounded, the product error decomposes into bounded multiples of the operand errors plus their product, giving
\[
e_{uv,k}=O\bigl(\delta_k^{\min\{p,q\}}\bigr).
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For bounded operands, recursive sums, differences, and products inherit at least the slower convergence order of their operand relaxations.
knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic Rate Inheritance

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated minimum-order inheritance is plausible for specific standard recursive formulas under uniform boundedness, and the property kind fits the container. However, "standard interval-consistent arithmetic rules" does not uniquely specify formulas sufficient for the result, and no source supplies the missing hypotheses or validates the product-error decomposition.

children.title: Composition Rate Inheritance
children.top_down_role: Convergence-order propagation through univariate and multivariate composition.

assumptions_latex: \(g:B_k\to D\subset\mathbb R^m\) has estimator or graph error \(O(\delta_k^q)\).
\(h:D\to\mathbb R\) is Lipschitz on a neighborhood containing all relevant image enclosures.
The outer relaxation of \(h\) on those enclosures has error \(O(\delta_k^r)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(e_{h\circ g,k}=O(\delta_k^{\min\{q,r\}})\).
review_flags: The multivariate graph-error formulation and enclosure hypotheses need a composition-relaxation source.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lipschitz outer mappings with separately controlled outer-envelope and inner-mapping errors.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the inner relaxation error be \(O(\delta_k^q)\), and let the relaxation error contributed by convexifying \(h\) on the chosen image enclosure be \(O(\delta_k^r)\). If \(h\) is Lipschitz there with a constant independent of \(k\), then the recursive composite error satisfies
\[
e_{h\circ g,k}\le C_1\delta_k^q+C_2\delta_k^r
=O\bigl(\delta_k^{\min\{q,r\}}\bigr).
\]

knowledge_statements.title: Arithmetic Subgradient Families
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Propagation rules for arithmetic nodes after valid convex and concave relaxations have been selected.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let operand relaxations on a convex set \(D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^n\) be \(u_i^{\mathrm{cv}}\) and \(u_i^{\mathrm{cc}}\). Scalar multiplication by \(a\) preserves the families when \(a\geq0\) and exchanges convex and concave families when \(a<0\). If its chosen argument functions \(v_i\) satisfy the required coordinatewise monotonicity and \(\alpha\in\partial H(v_1(x),v_2(x))\), then \(\alpha_1g_1+\alpha_2g_2\) is the corresponding propagated subgradient whenever \(g_i\in\partial v_i(x)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Topological Evaluation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single-pass relaxation evaluation in a dependency-respecting order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite directed acyclic factor graph \(G=(V,E)\), leaf relaxation records, and one valid transfer rule for each operation node. Compute a topological ordering \((v_1,\ldots,v_{|V|})\). Process nodes in that order: retain each leaf record, and at an operation node \(v_k\), read the already computed records of all predecessors, apply the node’s transfer rule, and store the result. Stop after the last root-reachable node and return the requested root records. Because every edge \((v_i,v_j)\in E\) satisfies \(i<j\), no operation is evaluated before its operands. If each node is processed once, the graph-management work is \(O(|V|+|E|)\), excluding the costs of primitive transfer rules.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A topological ordering ensures every operand record exists before its consumer is evaluated; one-pass graph-management cost is linear in nodes and edges.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a directed acyclic factor graph with stable node identities and a cache keyed by a node identity, domain-state identifier, relaxation-rule version, and required output fields. During topological evaluation, query the cache before processing node \(v\). On an exact key hit, return the stored range, relaxation, and sensitivity record. On a miss, evaluate \(v\) once from its predecessor records, store the complete result under that key, and supply the same immutable record to every consumer. Thus a shared subexpression represented by one graph node is evaluated at most once for each key, without altering the recursively defined relaxation returned at any root.

Mark every node in \(S\) dirty and propagate the mark along outgoing edges to all reachable descendants; leave every other valid cache entry unchanged. Process the dirty induced subgraph in an order inherited from a global topological ordering. At each dirty node, recompute its record from current predecessor records and replace its cache entry. Stop after all dirty requested roots have been updated. If transfer rules are deterministic functions of their recorded inputs and state, the resulting root records equal those obtained by complete reevaluation under the new state.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Changes invalidate affected nodes and descendants only; recomputing that induced subgraph in topological order matches a full deterministic reevaluation.
assumptions_latex: The graph structure remains acyclic and unchanged during the update.
Every changed state component is represented in \(S\) or its cache key.
Node transfer rules are deterministic from current predecessor records and rule state.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Incrementally updated root records equal full-reevaluation records, while only dirty nodes and their incident dependency edges require traversal.

knowledge_statements.title: Outward-Rounding Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Operationwise validated interval evaluation under finite-precision arithmetic.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be a factorable expression and \(X\) an interval box contained in its domain. For every elementary node function \(\psi\) and every interval argument tuple \(Y\) arising during evaluation, the interface must return an interval \(\widehat{\mathcal I}_\psi(Y)\) satisfying \(\{\psi(y):y\in Y\}\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal I}_\psi(Y)\). Its finite endpoints, constants, and conversions are computed with rounding toward \(-\infty\) for lower bounds and toward \(+\infty\) for upper bounds. Applying these inclusion-preserving interfaces at every node of the expression graph yields a computed enclosure \(\widehat F(X)\) satisfying \(F(X)=\{F(x):x\in X\}\subseteq\widehat F(X)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every elementary interval operation must enclose its exact node range, with lower endpoints rounded downward and upper endpoints rounded upward. Recursive use of these interfaces encloses every exact value of the factorable expression on the input box.

\(X\) is an interval box on which every evaluated intrinsic node is contained in its mathematical domain.
The floating-point environment provides directed rounding for all endpoint operations, constants, and conversions used by the interval interfaces.

assumptions_latex: Each original variable satisfies finite bounds \(l_i<u_i\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Positive diagonal affine scaling of bounded variables in factorable models.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Choose \(c_i\in\mathbb R\) and \(s_i>0\), and set \(x_i=c_i+s_i y_i\). Then \(y_i=(x_i-c_i)/s_i\), so the substitution is bijective. The original interval \([l_i,u_i]\) becomes \([(l_i-c_i)/s_i,(u_i-c_i)/s_i]\); choosing \(c_i=l_i\) and \(s_i=u_i-l_i\) maps it to \([0,1]\). Replacing every occurrence of \(x_i\) in the objective and constraints by \(c_i+s_i y_i\) yields an equivalent optimization problem, provided all factor domains and constants are transformed consistently.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive affine change of variables bijectively maps bounded variables to normalized coordinates and yields an equivalent factorable optimization problem after consistent substitution.

knowledge_statements.title: Factor Conditioning
knowledge_statements.scope_note: First-order absolute conditioning of a continuously differentiable scalar factor over a compact convex argument region.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) be open, let \(Y\subset U\) be compact and convex, and let \(\phi:U\to\mathbb R\) be continuously differentiable. For a fixed norm \(\|\cdot\|\) on \(\mathbb R^m\) and its dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\), define the absolute condition bound by \(\kappa_{\mathrm{abs}}(\phi,Y)=\max_{y\in Y}\|\nabla\phi(y)\|_*\). Then, for all \(y_1,y_2\in Y\), \(|\phi(y_2)-\phi(y_1)|\le\kappa_{\mathrm{abs}}(\phi,Y)\|y_2-y_1\|\). Relative conditioning requires separately specified nonzero argument and output scales.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a continuously differentiable scalar factor on a compact convex region, the absolute condition bound is the maximum dual norm of its gradient. It bounds output changes by the corresponding argument perturbation norm; relative conditioning additionally requires nonzero reference scales.
assumptions_latex: \(U\subseteq\mathbb R^m\) is open.
\(Y\subset U\) is compact and convex.
\(\phi:U\to\mathbb R\) is continuously differentiable.
A norm \(\|\cdot\|\) on arguments and its dual norm \(\|\cdot\|_*\) are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\kappa_{\mathrm{abs}}(\phi,Y)=\max_{y\in Y}\|\nabla\phi(y)\|_*\) and \(|\phi(y_2)-\phi(y_1)|\le\kappa_{\mathrm{abs}}(\phi,Y)\|y_2-y_1\|\) for all \(y_1,y_2\in Y\).

children.title: Scale-Induced Numerical Degradation
children.top_down_role: Reliability losses associated with poorly matched numerical scales.

assumptions_latex: Floating-point arithmetic has unit roundoff \(u\).
A computed graph evaluation accumulates local backward or rounding perturbations of size proportional to \(u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Scaling cannot be treated as numerically neutral: large condition amplification can make enclosure width or evaluation error large relative to the required tolerance.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: first-order rounding-error analysis predicts relative error proportional to unit roundoff times a condition measure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Failure regime caused by poor scaling and amplified floating-point perturbations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: With characteristic scales \(S_x>0\) and \(S_f>0\), define \(\kappa_{\mathrm{rel}}=(S_x/S_f)\kappa_{\mathrm{abs}}\). First-order floating-point analysis predicts an output perturbation of order \(u\kappa_{\mathrm{rel}}\) times graph-dependent accumulation factors. Consequently, when \(u\kappa_{\mathrm{rel}}\) is not small relative to the requested relative tolerance, computed bounds may become dominated by rounding inflation, cancellation, overflow, or underflow. Equivalent exact reformulations obtained by variable scaling can therefore have materially different numerical reliability, despite identical mathematical feasible sets and objective values.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Poor scales amplify rounding, cancellation, overflow, or underflow; mathematically equivalent scaled formulations can therefore produce very different enclosure quality and reliability.
knowledge_statements.title: Scale-Induced Numerical Degradation

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary kind and qualitative warning fit the container, but the graph-dependent first-order error assertion lacks a specified error model and supporting locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition-Model Growth
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit Cartesian partition models; formulation-specific sharing may reduce variable or constraint counts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Partitioning coordinate \(i\) into \(p_i\ge 1\) intervals produces \(P=\prod_{i=1}^d p_i\) Cartesian cells when every interval combination is represented explicitly. Hence a uniform partition with \(p_i=p\) has \(P=p^d\), which is exponential in the number \(d\) of jointly partitioned variables. If every cell contributes at most \(q\) local relations and at most \(r\) cell-specific variables, direct enumeration adds at most \(qP\) relations and \(rP\) variables, excluding shared base-model objects and encoding-dependent objects.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An explicit Cartesian refinement creates the product of the per-variable interval counts, so a uniform partition has p to the d cells. If each cell contributes at most q local relations and r cell-specific variables, direct enumeration adds at most q times P relations and r times P variables, apart from shared and encoding-dependent objects.

For each \(i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}\), coordinate \(i\) is divided into \(p_i\in\mathbb N\) intervals with \(p_i\ge 1\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Single separation and cut-materialization round for a current relaxation solution; reoptimization and solver-factorization maintenance are excluded.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a current relaxation solution, inspect \(M\) eligible relaxation objects. For object \(j\), let \(s_j\) be its separation cost, let \(k_j\) be the number of accepted cuts it emits, and let \(b_j\) be the total number of stored coefficient incidences in those cuts. Under constant-time storage per row header and coefficient incidence, one enrichment round costs \(O(M+\sum_{j=1}^M s_j+K+B)\), where \(K=\sum_{j=1}^M k_j\) and \(B=\sum_{j=1}^M b_j\). knowledge_statements.title: Enrichment-Cost Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto criterion balancing stronger lower bounds against outer-model evaluation and maintenance cost.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal E\) be a family of valid enrichments of a relaxation, let \(\beta(E)\) be the resulting lower bound for a fixed minimization subproblem, and let \(C(E)\ge 0\) measure construction, solution, and maintenance cost. Enrichment \(E_2\) dominates \(E_1\) when \(\beta(E_2)\ge\beta(E_1)\), \(C(E_2)\le C(E_1)\), and at least one inequality is strict. The enrichment-cost frontier is \[\mathcal P=\{E\in\mathcal E:\text{ no }E'\in\mathcal E\text{ dominates }E\}.\] A cost-efficient enrichment policy selects only members of \(\mathcal P\), possibly subject to a prescribed cost budget.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An enrichment is cost-efficient only if no alternative gives an equally strong or stronger bound at equal or lower evaluation and maintenance cost.
assumptions_latex: \(\beta(E)\) is a valid lower bound for every \(E\in\mathcal E\).
\(C(E)\) is measured consistently across enrichments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(E\text{ is cost-efficient}\Longrightarrow E\in\mathcal P\).

total computational cost of enrichment E

children.title: Convex Subproblem Bounds

knowledge_statements.title: Convex Subproblem Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity certificate for lower bounds obtained by minimizing a convex relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the minimization problem \(v=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\), where \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). Let \(C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be convex with \(F\subseteq C\), and let \(g:C\to\mathbb R\cup\{+\infty\}\) be convex and satisfy \(g(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). If the convex subproblem returns \(\beta=\inf_{x\in C}g(x)\), then \[\beta\le v.\] Thus the pair \((C,g)\), together with the computed subproblem value, certifies a valid global lower bound on the original subproblem.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing a convex underestimator over a convex superset of the feasible region produces a valid lower bound on the original minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq C\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) and \(C\) is convex.
\(g\) is convex on \(C\) and \(g(x)\le f(x)\) for all \(x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{x\in C}g(x)\le\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\).

notation.meaning: convex relaxation of the feasible set

children.title: Polyhedral Outer Bounds
children.top_down_role: Lower-bound values supplied by linear outer models.

knowledge_statements.title: Polyhedral Outer Bounds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Validity certificate for lower bounds returned by a linear outer model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(v=\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\) be a minimization problem, where \(F\subseteq\mathbb R^n\). Suppose the polyhedron \(P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\) contains \(F\), and the affine function \(\ell(x)=c^{\mathsf T}x+d\) satisfies \(\ell(x)\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\). Then the linear-program value \(\beta_P=\inf_{x\in P}\ell(x)\) satisfies \[\beta_P\le v.\] Thus a certified value of this linear outer model supplies a valid global lower bound whenever the inclusion and underestimation conditions have also been established.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Minimizing an affine underestimator over a polyhedral superset of the original feasible region yields a valid lower bound on the original minimum.
assumptions_latex: \(F\subseteq P=\{x\in\mathbb R^n:Ax\le b\}\).
\(\ell(x)=c^{\mathsf T}x+d\le f(x)\) for every \(x\in F\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\beta_P=\inf_{x\in P}\ell(x)\le\inf_{x\in F}f(x)\).

children.title: Refinement-Consistency Interfaces
children.top_down_role: Convergence properties required by external partition algorithms.

knowledge_statements.title: Refinement-Consistency Interfaces
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Local consistency condition required when a partition algorithm shrinks subregions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every compact region \(D\subseteq\mathbb R^n\), let \(\beta(D)\) be the relaxation lower bound and let \(v(D)=\inf\{f(x):x\in F\cap D\}\), with \(v(D)<+\infty\). The lower-bound interface is refinement-consistent if \(\beta(D)\le v(D)\) for every such \(D\), and for every nested sequence \(D_{k+1}\subseteq D_k\) with \(F\cap D_k\ne\varnothing\) and \(\operatorname{diam}(D_k)\to0\), \[v(D_k)-\beta(D_k)\longrightarrow0.\] Hence relaxation error vanishes along every feasible sequence of indefinitely refined partition elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A refinement-consistent interface remains valid and makes its local lower-bound gap vanish whenever nested feasible regions shrink to a point.
assumptions_latex: \(f:F\to\mathbb R\) is finite on each considered set \(F\cap D\).
\(D_k\) are compact, nested, feasible regions with \(\operatorname{diam}(D_k)\to0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(v(D_k)-\beta(D_k)\to0\).

children.title: Factorable Scope-Failure Taxonomy
children.top_down_role: Regimes where recursive factorable relaxations weaken, require domain decomposition, or fall outside their explicit-composition scope.

children.title: Representation Pathologies
children.top_down_role: Weakness caused by the selected expression representation.

children.title: Repeated-Dependency Inflation
children.top_down_role: Loss of range and relaxation strength from repeated variable occurrences.

knowledge_statements.title: Repeated-Dependency Inflation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical interval-evaluation failure caused by treating repeated occurrences independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[0,1]\) and consider the factorable expression \(f(x)=x-x\). Its exact range is \[f([0,1])=\{0\}.\] Natural interval evaluation treats the two syntactic occurrences independently and computes \[[0,1]-[0,1]=[-1,1].\] Thus the enclosure width is \(2\), although the true range width is \(0\). The inflation disappears only when the shared dependence of both occurrences on the same variable is retained or the expression is simplified before relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For x minus itself on [0,1], independent interval propagation returns [-1,1] although the exact range is the singleton {0}.
assumptions_latex: Each occurrence is evaluated by ordinary interval subtraction without dependency tracking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{range}(x-x)=\{0\}\subsetneq[-1,1]\).

notation.meaning: exact image of the interval under f

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample is correct and fits repeated-dependency inflation, but it has no cited evidence.

children.title: Unfavorable Product Grouping
children.top_down_role: Weak multilinear relaxations caused by recursive grouping choices.

knowledge_statements.title: Unfavorable Product Grouping
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Criterion identifying a recursive multilinear grouping that yields a weaker bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(w=x_1x_2x_3\) on a bounded box \(B\). Construct \(R_{(12)3}\) by introducing \(u=x_1x_2\), applying a bilinear convexification to \(u=x_1x_2\), and then convexifying \(w=ux_3\). Define \(R_{1(23)}\) analogously using \(v=x_2x_3\). For a linear objective \(q\), grouping \((12)3\) is unfavorable relative to \(1(23)\) precisely when \[\inf_{z\in R_{(12)3}}q(z)<\inf_{z\in R_{1(23)}}q(z),\] after both lifted sets are represented in a common comparison space. The strict inequality records a weaker minimization bound caused solely by recursive grouping.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A recursive product grouping is unfavorable when its lifted bilinear relaxation gives a strictly lower bound than another grouping of the same product.
assumptions_latex: \(B\subset\mathbb R^3\) is a box with finite coordinate bounds.
Both recursive formulations use the same valid bilinear convexification rule.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\inf_{R_{(12)3}}q<\inf_{R_{1(23)}}q\Longrightarrow (12)3\text{ is unfavorable for }q.\)

notation.meaning: recursive relaxation grouping the first two factors
recursive relaxation grouping the last two factors
linear objective used to compare bound strength

children.title: Lost Common Subexpressions
children.top_down_role: Independent relaxation of factors that share hidden dependencies.

knowledge_statements.title: Lost Common Subexpressions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A shared-expression example showing inflation after dependent copies are relaxed independently.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(x\in[0,1]\) and consider two occurrences of the same subexpression in \(f(x)=x-x\). If they are represented by a shared auxiliary variable \(y=x\), then \(f=y-y=0\). If common-subexpression identity is discarded and the occurrences are replaced only by independent range variables \(y,z\in[0,1]\), the relaxed expression becomes \(y-z\) with range \([-1,1]\). Therefore losing the equality \(y=z\) enlarges the projected value set from \(\{0\}\) to \([-1,1]\), despite unchanged individual factor ranges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replacing a shared subexpression by independent bounded copies loses their equality and can enlarge an exact singleton range to a nontrivial interval.
assumptions_latex: The copied variables retain only their individual bounds and not the linking equality \(y=z\).

notation.meaning: separate copies of a formerly shared subexpression

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The counterexample correctly isolates the loss of a linking equality and fits the leaf, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Excessive Lifting
children.top_down_role: Large extended models without commensurate strengthening.

knowledge_statements.title: Excessive Lifting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Model-size growth from redundant auxiliaries that leave the projected relaxation unchanged.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) be a nonempty relaxation containing a scalar component \(x_i\). For every integer \(m\ge1\), form the lifted set \[R_m=\{(x,y_1,\ldots,y_m):x\in R,\ y_j=x_i\text{ for }j=1,\ldots,m\}.\] Its projection satisfies \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R_m)=R\), so every objective depending only on \(x\) has exactly the same relaxation bound over \(R_m\) as over \(R\). Nevertheless, the formulation adds \(m\) variables and \(m\) linking equalities. Thus representation size grows without strengthening the relaxation in the original-variable space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Redundant lifted copies can add arbitrarily many variables and equations while leaving the projected feasible set and every original-variable bound unchanged.
assumptions_latex: \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^n\) is nonempty.
The optimization objective depends only on \(x\), not on the auxiliary copies.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{proj}_x(R_m)=R\) for every \(m\ge1\), while formulation size grows linearly in \(m\).

notation.meaning: relaxation augmented by m redundant copies

children.title: Domain Pathologies

children.title: Unbounded Factor Ranges
children.top_down_role: Primitive convexifications lacking the finite bounds they require.

knowledge_statements.title: Unbounded Factor Ranges
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite-bound requirement for standard bilinear convexification formulas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(w=xy\) with finite bounds \(x\in[x^L,x^U]\) and \(y\in[y^L,y^U]\), the standard bilinear McCormick relaxation is \[\begin{aligned}w&\ge x^Ly+y^Lx-x^Ly^L,\\w&\ge x^Uy+y^Ux-x^Uy^U,\\w&\le x^Uy+y^Lx-x^Uy^L,\\w&\le x^Ly+y^Ux-x^Ly^U.\end{aligned}\] These inequalities use every endpoint as a finite coefficient. If any member of \(\{x^L,x^U,y^L,y^U\}\) is infinite, this finite-box formula is not directly defined, so finite factor bounds or a different relaxation construction are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The standard four McCormick inequalities for a bilinear factor use finite lower and upper bounds for both factors; an infinite endpoint makes the finite-box formula inapplicable.
assumptions_latex: The relaxation uses the standard four finite-box bilinear inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{x^L,x^U,y^L,y^U\}\not\subset\mathbb R\Longrightarrow\text{the finite-box bilinear formula is not directly defined}.\)

notation.meaning: lower and upper bounds for x
lower and upper bounds for y

children.title: Singularity-Crossing Domains

knowledge_statements.title: Singularity-Crossing Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reciprocal factor on an interval crossing its pole.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(f(x)=1/x\) with a proposed interval domain \(D=[-1,1]\). The factor is undefined at \(x=0\), and \(f(x)\to-\infty\) as \(x\uparrow0\) from the left. Consequently, no finite real-valued convex function \(g\) on all of \(D\) can satisfy \(g(x)\le1/x\) for every \(x\in D\setminus\{0\}\). A valid finite relaxation must first exclude the pole and partition the natural domain into sign-consistent components, or otherwise represent the domain disjunctively.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The reciprocal on [-1,1] crosses a pole and admits no finite convex underestimator over the entire interval; subdivision or disjunction is required.
assumptions_latex: A finite real-valued convex underestimator is required on all of \(D\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nexists g:D\to\mathbb R\text{ convex such that }g(x)\le 1/x\text{ for all }x\in D\setminus\{0\}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The reciprocal example and its no-finite-convex-underestimator conclusion are mathematically coherent and fit the domain-pathology leaf, but no source is supplied.

children.title: Disconnected Natural Domains

knowledge_statements.title: Disconnected Natural Domains
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Intrinsic function whose natural domain splits inside the working interval.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=\log(x^2-1)\) and impose \(x\in[-2,2]\). Its natural domain within the box is \[D=[-2,-1)\cup(1,2],\] which is disconnected. Any single interval containing both components also contains \([-1,1]\), where the logarithm argument is nonpositive and \(f\) is not real-valued. Hence a factor relaxation defined only on interval domains cannot cover both components as one valid primitive relaxation; it must subdivide the box or introduce a disjunction selecting a component.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For log(x²−1) on [-2,2], the real domain has two components, so one interval relaxation necessarily includes invalid points.
assumptions_latex: \(f(x)=\log(x^2-1)\) is interpreted as a real-valued function.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{dom}(f)\cap[-2,2]=[-2,-1)\cup(1,2]\), requiring subdivision or disjunction for interval-based convexification.

notation.meaning: natural domain inside the working interval

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The stated real domain is correct and the counterexample fits the leaf, but the claimed subdivision-or-disjunction requirement for interval-based convexification lacks cited support.

children.title: Regularity Pathologies

children.title: Boundary Subgradient Failure
children.top_down_role: Loss of propagated sensitivity information when boundary regularity is absent.

knowledge_statements.title: Boundary Subgradient Failure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Convex boundary point with no finite supporting subgradient.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(f(x)=-\sqrt{x}\) on \([0,1]\). This function is convex, but its convex subdifferential at the boundary point \(0\) is empty. Indeed, a finite subgradient \(g\in\mathbb R\) would require \[-\sqrt{y}\ge f(0)+g(y-0)=gy\qquad\text{for every }y\in[0,1].\] For \(y>0\), this implies \(g\le-1/\sqrt{y}\), which no finite \(g\) satisfies as \(y\downarrow0\). Therefore a propagation rule requiring a finite boundary subgradient cannot produce an affine support there.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex function −√x has no finite subgradient at zero, so finite-slope affine-support propagation fails at that boundary.
assumptions_latex: Subgradients are required to be finite real numbers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\partial f(0)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: convex subdifferential of f at zero

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The boundary subgradient counterexample is correct for the convex function on the stated domain and fits the regularity-pathology leaf, but no authoritative source is supplied.

children.title: Discontinuous Factors

knowledge_statements.title: Discontinuous Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete obstruction to exact continuous factor relaxations at a jump.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(h(x)=\mathbf{1}_{[0,\infty)}(x)\). For every \(a>0\) and every pair of continuous functions \(\ell,u:[-a,a]\to\mathbb{R}\) satisfying \(\ell(x)\le h(x)\le u(x)\) for all \(x\in[-a,a]\), one has \(u(0)-\ell(0)\ge 1\). Hence the continuous relaxation gap at the jump does not vanish as \(a\downarrow0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every continuous lower and upper relaxation of the step function has gap at least one at its jump, even on symmetrically shrinking intervals.
assumptions_latex: \(\ell,u:[-a,a]\to\mathbb{R}\) are continuous and satisfy \(\ell\le h\le u\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u(0)-\ell(0)\ge 1\) for every \(a>0\).

notation.meaning: Step factor with its jump value assigned to the upper branch

children.title: Highly Oscillatory Factors

knowledge_statements.title: Highly Oscillatory Factors
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Frequency-indexed failure of fixed-complexity monotonicity or curvature partitioning.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each integer \(k\ge1\), let \(h_k(x)=\sin(kx)\) on \(D=[0,2\pi]\). The factor has \(2k+1\) maximal monotonicity intervals, and its curvature changes sign at the \(2k-1\) interior points \(x=j\pi/k\), \(j=1,\ldots,2k-1\). Consequently, any interval partition on which both derivative and curvature signs are fixed requires a number of cells growing at least linearly with \(k\); no uniformly bounded number of such cells represents all members of the family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Increasing-frequency sine factors have linearly many monotonicity and curvature regions, so no fixed-size sign-consistent partition represents the entire family.
assumptions_latex: \(k\in\mathbb{N}\) and \(k\ge1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The number of cells required to keep derivative and curvature signs fixed is \(\Omega(k)\).
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: zeros of the first and second derivatives give the stated region counts

knowledge_statements.title: Wide-Domain Degradation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical quantitative example of primitive relaxation degradation on expanding boxes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For the bilinear factor \(w=xy\) on \((x,y)\in[-R,R]^2\), where \(R>0\), the McCormick convex and concave envelopes at \((x,y)=(0,0)\) have values \(-R^2\) and \(R^2\), respectively. Their vertical separation is therefore \(2R^2\), although the true factor value is \(0\). Thus the absolute center width grows quadratically with the domain radius.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a square of radius R, the McCormick relaxation of a bilinear factor has center width two R squared, so its absolute width grows quadratically with domain size.

assumptions_latex: Each scalar factor \(f_i\) is Lipschitz on the propagated interval with constant \(L_i\).
The relaxation introduced at stage \(i\) has local deviation at most \(\delta_i\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The terminal deviation can reach the scale \(\sum_{j=1}^{m}\delta_j\prod_{r=j+1}^{m}L_r\), so depth-independent tightness requires additional contraction or reformulation.

notation.meaning: Lipschitz constant of the stage factor

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: repeated application of the displayed Lipschitz error recurrence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stagewise error propagation along a scalar factorable composition path.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider \(z_i=f_i(z_{i-1})\) for \(i=1,\ldots,m\). If a relaxed state has deviation \(E_{i-1}\) before stage \(i\), Lipschitz propagation plus a local relaxation deviation \(\delta_i\) gives \(E_i\le L_iE_{i-1}+\delta_i\). With \(E_0=0\), iteration yields \(E_m\le\sum_{j=1}^{m}\delta_j\prod_{r=j+1}^{m}L_r\), where an empty product equals \(1\). This bound can grow with depth, and examples with aligned affine perturbations attain equality. Thus local accuracy alone does not ensure a depth-independent terminal gap.
